Answer A: Dr. Carlson may or may not be violating ethical guidelines, depending on the circumstances.
Answer B: The fact that Marla initiated the potential relationship is not relevant.
Answer D: As long as Dr. Carlson does not have "supervisory, evaluative, or other authority" over Marla, it would not be a violation of ethical
guidelines if he becomes sexually involved with her (see Standards 3.08 and 7.07 of the APA's Ethics Code and Principle II.28 of the Canadian
Code of Ethics). Personal relationships with students might be prohibited by university policy, but this question is asking about ethical
guidelines.

questions.question: A couple brings their ten-year-old son to therapy at the suggestion of his school counselor, who is concerned because the boy has started arguing with his teacher and getting into physical �ghts with his classmates. After several sessions with the boy and his family, you receive a letter from the school principal requesting information about the boy's condition, and a signed release from the boy's parents is included with the letter. As an ethical psychologist, you should:

options.A: refuse to release the records to anyone but a licensed psychologist.
options.B: refuse to release the records to anyone but the boy's parents.
options.C: release only that information you believe to be relevant to the school's concerns.
options.D: release photocopies of your complete �le on the boy and his family.

questions.explanation:
Since the boy's parents have signed a release, you would ordinarily provide information to the school principal, but not necessarily all of the
information available. The most ethical course of action in this situation would be to release only information that is relevant to the school's
role in the boy's treatment. Doing so would be consistent with the provisions of Standard 4.04(a) of the APA's Ethics Code, which states that
written and oral reports include "only information germane to the purpose for which the communication is made." It is also consistent with the
provisions of Principles I.37 and 39 of the Canadian Code of Ethics.
Answer A: It is not always practical or necessary to limit communication to another psychologist. In this case, the parents seem to believe the
psychologist has helpful information to offer school personnel.
Answer B: In signing the release, the parents are consenting to a degree of communication between the identi�ed parties.
Answer D: The psychologist is ethically bound to release the information relevant to the concerns of school personnel.

questions.question: Students in an introductory psychology class are required to participate in one of the university's ongoing research projects. This practice is:

options.A: ethical as long as students can choose to participate in an alternative activity instead.
options.B: ethical as long as students are free to choose the research project they participate in.
options.C: ethical as long as informed consent is obtained from students before they participate.

questions.explanation:
This issue is addressed by Standard 8.04 of the APA's Ethics Code and Principle I.36 of the Canadian Code of Ethics. Standard 8.04(b), for
example, states that "when research participation is a course requirement or an opportunity for extra credit, the prospective participant is given
the choice of equitable alternative activities."
Answer B: This is incorrect, as the ethical guidelines state that students need to have the option of an alternative assignment if they do not
want to serve as a research participant.
Answer C: Even though informed consent is required for research participants, this answer does not address the ethical concern involved in
requiring students to participate.
Answer D: Having the option to participate in research can be a learning opportunity for students, provided that they are not required to do so
when there are no other options.

questions.question: The 1976 Tarasoff decision established:

options.A: the right of a parent to inspect and request modi�cations to their child's school records.
options.B: a psychologist's duty to protect the intended victim of a therapy client.
options.C: the 80% rule as a standard for determining the fairness of a selection test or other employment procedure.
options.D: a psychologist's duty to report suspected or known cases of child abuse.

questions.explanation:
The Tarasoff decision established that, under certain circumstances, client con�dentiality must be breached when the client is a danger to
others. Although the original 1974 Tarasoff decision established a "duty to warn" the intended victim of a therapy client, that decision was
superseded by the 1976 rehearing of the case, which established a "duty to protect" the intended victim. Speci�cally, the 1976 ruling states that
a psychotherapist has a duty to protect an intended victim of a therapy client by warning "the intended victim or others likely to apprise the
victim of the danger, . . . [notifying] the police, or . . . [taking] whatever other steps are reasonably necessary under the circumstances."
Additional information on the ruling is provided in the Ethics Manual.
Answer A: The Buckley Amendment deals with parental rights to inspect and revise school records.
Answer C: The Tarasoff decision deals with a client who is a danger to another.
Answer D: The Tarasoff decision is not restricted to child abuse.

questions.question: When a psychologist learns that a colleague has committed an ethical violation, the psychologist:

options.A: may choose to ignore the violation if it is unlikely to be repeated by the colleague.
options.B: must report the violation to the Ethics Committee or state/provincial licensing board.
options.C: may attempt to resolve the situation informally by discussing it with the colleague if it seems appropriate to do so.
options.D: should contact the colleague's client to ascertain that a violation has actually occurred before taking any further action.

questions.explanation:
Ethical guidelines require psychologists to take action when they learn that a colleague has committed an ethical violation. This may involve
addressing the issue informally when it seems appropriate to do so or reporting the violation to the Ethics Committee or licensing board when
it does not seem appropriate for, or has not been resolved adequately through, informal resolution. This issue is addressed in Standards 1.04
and 1.05 of the APA's Ethics Code and Principles II.41 and II.42 of the Canadian Code of Ethics.
Answer A: The ethical guidelines do not recommend ignoring unethical behavior in a colleague.
Answer B: This is incorrect as it states a psychologist MUST report the violation to the Ethics Committee or licensing board, which is not true,
especially if it can be resolved informally.
Answer D: Ethical guidelines do not recommend involving clients in investigating unethical behavior.

questions.question: The Ethics Committee is investigating a complaint against a psychologist and requests, by letter, that you provide the Committee with information about the complainant. The complainant is a former client of yours that you stopped seeing 9 years ago. As an ethical psychologist, you should:

options.A: respond immediately to the Committee's request by supplying the relevant information.
options.B: respond immediately to the Committee's request, but only provide information you believe is relevant to the complaint.
options.C: respond to the Committee's request by advising that the information you have is obsolete.
options.D: respond immediately to the Committee's request but only provide information after verifying that the former client has signed a release of information.

questions.explanation:
Standard 1.06 of APA's Ethics Code states that psychologists address issues related to con�dentiality and that they respond to inquiries from
Ethics Committees. This answer is consistent with the provisions of the ethical guidelines.
Answer A: To send information without a release of information would violate con�dentiality in this case.
Answer B: Providing information without a release would violate con�dentiality.
Answer C: If the information in the �le is obsolete, it would be important to note this in any response to the Ethics Committee. However, this
response fails to address the issue of con�dentiality.

questions.question: The owner of a small advertising agency refers an employee of the agency to Dr. K., a clinical psychologist, for an evaluation. The owner states that he believes the employee is "too thick-headed" to be a bene�t to the company. The owner and Dr. K. agree, prior to the evaluation, that the psychologist will report back to the owner and advise if additional training may improve the employee's job performance. The psychologist prepares a report for the owner after several sessions. The owner consequently decides to terminate the employee based on this report and the employee's previous work history. The employee is very upset with Dr. K. for not informing him about the purpose of the evaluation and proceeds to �le a complaint against Dr. K. with the Ethics Committee. The Committee is likely to:

options.A: dismiss the complaint since complaints can be �led only by the clients of psychologists (in this case, the owner) or by other psychologists.
options.B: dismiss the complaint since, in this situation, the psychologist could not reveal the purpose of the evaluation to the employee in order to obtain accurate information.
options.C: dismiss the complaint since the psychologist acted appropriately by providing information only to his client, the owner, who was responsible for informing the employee about the purpose of the evaluation.
options.D: �nd that the psychologist acted unethically by not informing the employee about the purpose of the evaluation.

questions.explanation:
Ethical Standard 3.07 states that "when psychologists agree to provide services to a person or entity at the request of a third party,
psychologists attempt to clarify at the outset of the service the nature of the relationship with all individuals or organizations involved. This
clari�cation includes the role of the psychologist (e.g., therapist, consultant, diagnostician, or expert witness), an identi�cation of who is the
client, the probable uses of the services provided or the information obtained, and the fact that there may be limits to con�dentiality." The
Ethics Committee censured a psychologist for not clearly explaining the purpose of the evaluation to the employee in an actual case that was
similar to this scenario (APA, 1987).
Answer A: There is no restriction regarding who can �le a complaint against a psychologist (except that complaints generally cannot be �led
anonymously).
Answer B: This is not consistent with the provisions of the Ethics Code, given that the psychologist did not explain at the outset the probable
uses of the information obtained.
Answer C: This is not consistent with the provisions of the Ethics Code, given that the psychologist did not clarify at the outset the nature of
relationships with all parties and the probable uses of the information obtained.

questions.question: Research on job satisfaction suggests that it:

options.A: is an enduring disposition that is minimally affected by job changes.
options.B: is unrelated to being treated equitably by one’s employer.
options.C: is a poor predictor of longevity.
options.D: has a positive correlation with turnover.

questions.explanation:
Research suggests job satisfaction is a stable trait that is minimally affected by changes in occupations and/or employers. This has been
supported by twin studies that indicate a genetic contribution to job satisfaction.
Answer B: Job satisfaction is related to employees’ perception of being treated equitably by their employer. Research suggests that equitable
treatment is more predictive of job satisfaction than is the actual level of pay.
Answer C: Research demonstrates that job satisfaction is a better predictor of longevity than either physical health or tobacco use.
Answer D: There is a negative correlation between job satisfaction and turnover (r = -.40), meaning that as measures of job satisfaction
increase, turnover rates decrease.

questions.question: A group's performance on a(n) ____________ task is limited by the performance of the least skilled or knowledgeable member of the group.
questions.explanation:
Group tasks are categorized as additive, compensatory, disjunctive, or conjunctive. On a conjunctive task, the performance of the least
competent member places a limit on the group's product or performance. Mountain climbing is an example of a conjunctive task.
Answer A: On additive tasks, the coordinated efforts of several people add together to form the group product.
Answer B: When performing a compensatory task, the average of the contributions of all members of the group represents the group product.
Answer C: On a disjunctive task, the solution of one member of the group is chosen by the group to be the group's solution.

questions.question: Expectancy theory predicts that worker motivation depends on several factors including "valence", which refers to:

options.A: the employee's beliefs about the value of rewards provided for successful performance.
options.B: the employee's beliefs about the inherent (intrinsic) value of the work itself.
options.C: the strength of the worker's motivation and organizational commitment.
options.D: the strength of the effort (versus ability) component of the worker's motivation.

questions.explanation:
According to expectancy theory, motivation is a function of three components: expectancy, instrumentality, and valence. For the exam, you
want to be familiar with the characteristics of all three components. Valence refers to the value a worker places on the outcomes that will be
provided for successful performance. When these outcomes have positive valence, this increases the worker's motivation to perform.
Answer B: Expectancy theory does not address the employee's beliefs about the inherent (intrinsic) value of the work itself.
Answer C: Expectancy theory does not address the strength of the worker's motivation and organizational commitment.
Answer D: Expectancy theory does not address the strength of the effort (versus ability) component of the worker's motivation.

questions.question: According to Fiedler's contingency model of leadership, high LPC (least preferred coworker) leaders:

options.A: are always more effective than low LPC leaders.
options.B: are more effective than low LPC leaders in moderately favorable situations.
options.C: elicit less trust from supervisees than do low LPC leaders.
options.D: elicit less intrinsic motivation from supervisees than do low LPC leaders.

questions.explanation:
According to Fiedler, low LPC leaders are most effective in low and high favorable situations, while high LPC leaders are most effective in
moderately favorable situations.
Answer A: Fielder's model of leadership is a contingency theory that proposes that leadership effectiveness is the result of an interaction
between the leader's style and the favorableness of the situation and will therefore vary according to this contingency, with high LPC leaders
being more effective in some situations and low LPC leaders being more effective in others.
Answer C: High LPC leaders are relationship-oriented and are concerned with maintaining supportive and trusting relationships with their
supervisees, but nothing in this theory assumes that the supervisees themselves reciprocate this trust.
Answer D: Fiedler studied leadership effectiveness, not the intrinsic motivation of employees, but implied that the ability of high and low LPC
leaders to foster the motivation of employees depends on the interaction between the leader's style and the nature of the situation.

questions.question: An organizational psychologist �nds that his newly developed selection test has different validity coe�cients for male and female applicants and that the difference is statistically signi�cant. This suggests that the test has:
questions.explanation:
For the exam, you should be familiar with all of the terms listed in the answers to this question. Additional information about these terms is
provided in the Industrial-Organizational Psychology chapter of the written study materials. The selection test described in this question has
different levels of validity for males and females—i.e., it has differential validity.
Answer A: A test's incremental validity refers to the bene�ts that use of the test provides with regard to decision-making accuracy.
Answer B: A test has discriminant (divergent) validity when it has low correlations with tests that measure different traits, characteristics, or
abilities. Discriminant validity provides evidence of a test's construct validity.
Answer D: A test has convergent validity when it correlates highly with tests that measure the same trait. Convergent validity provides evidence
of construct validity.

questions.question: In organizations, the 80% rule is used to determine if:

options.A: a selection procedure is having an adverse impact.
options.B: a selection procedure is cost effective.
options.C: a performance appraisal measure has adequate relevance.
options.D: a performance appraisal measure has adequate utility.

questions.explanation:
The 80% rule is described in the EEOC's Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures and is used to determine if a selection test or
other employment procedure is discriminating against members of a group protected by law. As de�ned by the 80% rule, a selection test is
having an adverse impact when the proportion of minority-group applicants who are selected is less than 80% of the proportion of majority-
group applicants who are selected.
Answer B: Cost effectiveness is irrelevant with regard to the 80% rule.
Answer C: Adequate relevance of a performance appraisal is not the de�ning attribute of the 80% rule.
Answer D: Adequate utility of a performance appraisal is not the de�ning attribute of the 80% rule.

questions.question: Lewin's force �eld theory describes planned change in organizations as involving which of the following stages?

options.D: Setting the stage, problem-solving, and reaching an agreement

questions.explanation:
According to Lewin (1951), organizations continuously respond to forces that either promote or resist change. Unfreezing, changing, and
refreezing are the three stages of planned change identi�ed by Lewin.
Answer B: These are not the three stages of planned change identi�ed by Lewin.
Answer C: These are not the three stages of planned change identi�ed by Lewin.
Answer D: These are the three stages of mediation.

questions.question: The primary purpose of a realistic job preview is to:

options.A: increase the number of applicants for a job.
options.C: reduce on-the-job con�icts between managers and employees.

questions.explanation:
Realistic job previews may consist of job descriptions, videos, discussions with current employees, work samples, and/or other procedures or
techniques. One assumption underlying the use of realistic job previews is that turnover is related to unrealistic expectations about the job.
Instead, providing applicants with accurate information about what the job entails will help to reduce unrealistic expectations and thereby
decrease dissatisfaction and turnover.
Answer A: A realistic job preview may actually decrease, not increase, the number of applicants for a job.
Answer B: It is not the purpose of a realistic job preview to develop an accurate job description.
Answer C: The purpose of a realistic job preview is to reduce unrealistic job expectations, not on-the-job con�icts between managers and
employees.

questions.question: Donald Super's ____________ graphically depicts the correspondence between an individual's life roles and life stages.
questions.explanation:
Super uses several pictures to illustrate elements of his life-space, life-span theory of career development. The life career rainbow relates the
individual's nine life roles (e.g., child, student, citizen) to �ve life stages (growth, exploration, establishment, maintenance, and disengagement).
Answer B: Super does not use a life staircase to depict components of his theory.
Answer C: Super does not use a mandala to depict his theory.
Answer D: Super does not use an octagon to illustrate elements of his theory (but Holland uses a hexagon to illustrate elements of his theory).

questions.question: A transformational leader uses "framing" in order to:

options.A: make the organization's goals more meaningful to employees.
options.B: clarify the consequences of undesirable performance.
options.D: adapt their leadership style to the characteristics of subordinates.

questions.explanation:
Even if you're unfamiliar with the term "framing," you may have been able to identify the correct answer with your knowledge of
transformational leadership. Transformational leaders recognize the need for change and are able to communicate that need to employees.
Framing is one technique these leaders use to inspire employees, and it involves describing the organization's goals in a way that makes them
more meaningful to employees.
Answer B: A transformational leader does not use framing to clarify the consequences of undesirable performance.
Answer C: The term "framing" is also used to refer to a type of decision-making bias. In that context, framing occurs when the description of a
problem in a positive or negative way in�uences the type of decision that is made. However, this question is asking about the use of framing by
transformational leaders.
Answer D: This response, if it included the leader utilizing a style that would not only adapt to the characteristics of the employee but to the
work environment as well, would be describing the Path-Goal Theory, not the transformational leader's use of framing.

questions.question: The best conclusion that can be drawn about the four-day (compressed) workweek is that it has:

options.A: long-lasting positive effects on attitudes and productivity.
options.B: long-lasting negative effects on attitudes and productivity.
options.C: positive effects on attitudes but little or no impact on productivity.
options.D: positive effects on attitudes initially but, over time, increasingly negative effects on both attitudes and productivity.

questions.explanation:
The compressed workweek requires employees to work a 4-day, 40-hour week. Overall, alternative work schedules have been found to have
more bene�cial effects on attitudes than on productivity, and this seems to be particularly true for the compressed workweek. For example, a
meta-analysis of the research on the compressed workweek by Baltes and his colleagues (1999) found an effect size of .59 for satisfaction
and .04 for productivity.
Answer A: The four-day (compressed) workweek does not have speci�c long-lasting effects of any kind.
Answer B: The four-day (compressed) workweek does not have speci�c long-lasting effects of any kind.
Answer D: The four-day (compressed) workweek does not have effects that change over time.

questions.question: According to Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership model, "employee maturity" is a function of the employee's:

options.C: skills and willingness to assume responsibility.
options.D: beliefs about the meaning and value of work.

questions.explanation:
Hersey and Blanchard propose that a leader is most effective when their behavior matches the employee's level of maturity. Hersey and
Blanchard distinguish between two aspects of employee maturity: job maturity refers to the employee's knowledge and skills, while
psychological maturity refers to the employee's self-con�dence and willingness to assume responsibility.
Answers A, B, and D: "Employee maturity" in this theory is considered a function of the employee's skills and willingness to assume
responsibility, not a function of the stage of career development, personality, or beliefs about the meaning and value of work.

questions.question: Assessment centers are most commonly used to:
questions.explanation:
Assessment centers were originally used during World War II as a means of selecting OSS agents. They are now used primarily for evaluating
and predicting the performance of managerial-level employees—particularly, evaluating managerial-level employees for the purpose of
selection, promotion, or training. Assessment centers have participants engage in a variety of exercises, many of which simulate the actual
tasks a manager performs on-the-job.
Answer A: Assessment centers are most commonly used to hire and promote managers, not clerical workers.
Answer C: Assessment centers are most commonly used to hire and promote managers, not to train semi-skilled and skilled workers.
Answer D: Assessment centers are most commonly used to hire and promote managers, not to train salespeople.

questions.question: In organizations, the "paired comparison" technique is used to:

options.D: determine the appropriate compensation for a job.

questions.explanation:
The paired comparison technique is a method of performance appraisal. See the Industrial-Organizational Psychology chapter for a description
of other speci�c methods that you're likely to encounter on the exam. As its name implies, use of the paired comparison technique involves
comparing each employee to every other employee in pairs on each dimension of job performance.
Answers B, C, and D: In organizations, the "paired comparison" technique is used to evaluate an employee's job performance, not make hiring
and placement decisions, identifying an employee's training needs, or determining the appropriate compensation for a job.

questions.question: The rational-economic model of decision making is based on the assumption that:

options.A: decision makers place more emphasis on the costs of certain decisions than on other consequences of their decisions.
options.B: decision makers have complete information about all alternatives and their consequences before making decisions.
options.C: individuals are better than groups at making decisions, especially under stressful conditions.
options.D: decision makers' knowledge about possible alternatives is always incomplete.

questions.explanation:
As its name implies, the rational-economic model assumes that decisions are based on a rational process. From the perspective of the
rational-economic model, "rational" means considering all alternatives and their consequences before making a decision.
Answer A: Decision makers' placement of more emphasis on the costs of certain decisions than on other consequences of their decisions is
not an assumption of the rational-economic model.
Answer C: The fact that individuals are better than groups at making decisions, especially under stressful conditions, is not an assumption of
this model.
Answer D. A criticism of the rational-economic model is that it does not take into account that a decision maker's knowledge about alternatives
is often incomplete.

questions.question: The primary purpose of a(n) ____________ is to obtain detailed information about job requirements in order to facilitate decisions related to compensation.
questions.explanation:
Of the procedures listed in the answers, only one is conducted speci�cally to facilitate decisions related to compensation. A job evaluation is
conducted speci�cally for the purpose of determining the relative worth of jobs in order to set wages and salaries. It does this by identifying
compensable factors such as skills and education, autonomy and responsibility, and the consequences of errors.
Answer A: A needs assessment is conducted to identify training needs.
Answer B: An organizational analysis is often part of a needs assessment and is conducted to identify the organization's goals.
Answer C: A job analysis is conducted to identify the essential characteristics of a job. Job analysis serves several functions in an organization
and may be the �rst step in a job evaluation.

questions.question: An organizational psychologist would most likely recommend the use of vestibule training for which of the following jobs?
questions.explanation:
Vestibule training involves the use of a simulated job environment. Vestibule training is used when on-the-job training would be too costly or
hazardous, as it would be in pilot training.
Answer B: Vestibule training would be inappropriate for training a word processor since on-the-job training would not be too costly or
hazardous for such a position.
Answer C: Vestibule training would be inappropriate for training a salesperson since on-the-job training would not be too costly or hazardous
for such a position.
Answer D: Vestibule training would be inappropriate for training a clinical psychologist since on-the-job training would not be too costly or
hazardous for such a position.

questions.question: If you were hired by a large company to develop a new training program, your �rst step would probably be to conduct a:
questions.explanation:
For the exam, you want to be able to distinguish among needs analysis, job analysis, and job evaluation. All three are described in the
Industrial-Organizational Psychology chapter of the written study materials. Training program development begins with a needs analysis (also
known as a needs assessment), which usually consists of three components: an organizational analysis, a job analysis, and a person analysis.
Answer B: A job evaluation is conducted to determine the appropriate compensation for a job.
Answer C: A summative evaluation is conducted to determine the effects of a training program or intervention after it has been developed.
Answer D: A formative evaluation is conducted while a training program or intervention is being developed to determine if modi�cations are
required in order for the program or intervention to achieve its goals.

questions.question: A manager who adheres to the principles of "scienti�c management" would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Employees view work as natural as play and actively seek autonomy and responsibility.
options.B: An employee's relationships with their coworkers are important determinants of job satisfaction.
options.C: Because employees value money more than other incentives, pay is the most effective motivator.
options.D: An employee's unful�lled needs take precedence over other needs, and rewards should be determined accordingly.

questions.explanation:
Scienti�c management was developed by Frederick Taylor (1911) who applied the scienti�c method to the study of job productivity. Taylor
believed that employees are motivated primarily by economic self-interest and, therefore, that money is the most effective motivator.
Answer A: This describes McGregor's Theory Y managers.
Answer B: This is an assumption of the human relations movement, which was an alternative to scienti�c management.
Answer D: This seems more akin to Maslow's need hierarchy theory.

questions.question: In the context of Holland's RIASEC model, ____________ refers to the difference in the magnitude of scores an examinee obtains on the six personality types.
questions.explanation:
All of the terms listed in the answers to this question refer to constructs that are important in Holland's theory. The question provides an
accurate description of differentiation. A highly differentiated person obtains a high score on one personality type and low scores on all other
types.
Answer A: In Holland's model, consistency refers to the similarity of the individual's primary interests (highest codes). For example, realistic and
enterprising are consistent, but realistic and social are not consistent.
Answer C: Vocational identity refers to the degree to which the individual has a clear and stable picture of his or her goals, interests, and
talents.
Answer D: Congruence refers to the degree of similarity between the person and the person's work environment.

questions.question: The highest levels of learning and performance are usually associated with:
questions.explanation:
Even if you're not familiar with the Yerkes-Dodson law (which proposes that learning and performance are curvilinearly related to arousal), you
may have been able to identify the correct answer on the basis of common sense—i.e., most people perform best when their level of arousal is
somewhere between "none" and "a lot." Moderate levels of arousal are associated with the highest levels of learning and performance. This is
particularly true when moderate levels of arousal are combined with moderate task di�culty.
Answer A: A low level of arousal can lead to boredom, which can negatively affect learning and performance.
Answer C: A high level of arousal can lead to stress and fatigue, which can negatively affect learning and performance.
Answer D: Varying levels of arousal would not be optimal for learning and performance.

questions.question: What is the best way to mitigate the halo effect?

options.C: Make the results of all assessments available to employees
options.D: Involve raters in the rating scale development process

questions.explanation:
Employee performance assessments frequently involve subjective measures that are associated with rater bias. One bias type is the halo
effect. The halo effect occurs when the rater's rating of an employee's job performance on one dimension affects performance ratings on other
dimensions. Rating scale training increases rating accuracy. Researchers have demonstrated that comprehensive training can mitigate the halo
effect. The halo effect and other rater bias types can also be reduced by employing multiple raters, by implementing behavior-speci�c ratings
(as opposed to ratings based on global behaviors), and by using speci�c scale types (such as forced-choice and paired comparison scales).
Answer B: Peer ratings have been identi�ed as reliable predictors of training success but have not proven effective for mitigating the halo
effect.
Answer C: Result availability enhances employee acceptance of the appraisal process but does not help to mitigate the halo effect.
Answer D: This does not represent a direct method of mitigating the halo effect. However, rater involvement in the overall rating process can
potentially increase accurate and thorough rating scale use.

questions.question: Which of the following would be LEAST useful for eliminating the halo effect, the central tendency bias, and other rater biases from performance ratings?
questions.explanation:
This question relies on the distinction between relative and absolute measures of employee performance. Absolute techniques used to
measure job performance are susceptible to a number of rater biases that limit their accuracies, such as the leniency/strictness bias, the
central tendency bias, and the halo effect (which can be positive or negative). The Likert scale is a subjective rating scale that is susceptible to
rater bias and may not provide accurate information pertaining to performance ratings. Likert-type scales and other graphic rating scales are
susceptible to rater bias, particularly when global dimensions are rated. The other answer options are examples of relative measures of
employee performance, where raters are required to compare two or more employees to each other. Relative techniques help alleviate rater
biases.
Answer A: The paired comparison technique is used when a rater compares each employee with every other employee, in pairs, on dimensions
of job performance.
Answer C: The forced distribution technique involves assigning employees to a limited number of categories based on prede�ned normal
distribution on one or more dimensions of job performance.
Answer D: Ranking employees is another relative technique used to mitigate rater bias. Employees may be ranked from highest to lowest on a
dimension of job performance (such as most to least productive).

questions.question: An employer can refuse to hire older workers:

options.A: only when there is a much larger proportion of younger than older job applicants.
options.B: when previous experience with an older worker has suggested that they cannot perform the job successfully.
options.C: when the employer hires older workers for other positions in the company.
options.D: when younger age is required due to the nature of the job.

questions.explanation:
Title VII and related legislation includes anti-discrimination exception requirements for instances wherein discrimination may be necessary for
the normal operation of the business. Age discrimination is acceptable if age is clearly a bona �de occupational quali�cation (BFOQ).
Disneyland HR personnel would likely not encounter EEOC resistance for employing only younger men for the position of "Prince Charming."
Answer A: This is not an acceptable reason for not hiring older workers.
Answer B: One or a few "bad experiences" would not be su�cient justi�cation for not hiring older workers.
Answer C: This is not considered an adequate remedy by anti-discrimination legislation.

questions.question: Which of the following do implosive therapy and �ooding have in common?

options.A: Both involve exposure to an unconditioned (aversive) stimulus.
options.C: Both involve the use of negative reinforcement.
options.D: Both lead to extinction of the undesirable response.

questions.explanation:
Implosive therapy and �ooding are both behavioral treatments that are premised on the principles of classical conditioning. The conditioned
response is eventually extinguished through exposure to the feared stimulus, either in vivo (as in �ooding) or in imagination (as in implosive
therapy).
Answer A: This answer is incorrect because the exposure is to the conditioned—not the unconditioned—stimulus in both treatments.
Answer B: Neither implosive therapy nor �ooding involves counterconditioning, which is a technique that is utilized in systematic
desensitization through use of relaxation techniques when anxiety-provoking stimuli are presented.
Answer C: Negative reinforcement is an operant conditioning term. This response is incorrect because both treatments are derived from
classical, not operant, conditioning.

questions.question: Bandura's social cognitive theory predicts that:

options.A: cognitive events act as intervening variables in the acquisition of a new behavior.
options.B: social approval is a powerful primary reinforcement.
options.C: reinforcement has a greater impact on learning than on performance.
options.D: the acquisition of new behaviors is the result of internalized S-R connections.

questions.explanation:
According to social learning theory, which was later reworked to be social cognitive theory; an individual learns a new behavior simply by
observing another person engaging in that behavior. Bandura concluded that observational learning involves four processes, which are critical
intervening variables in the acquisition of a new behavior: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. Attention (i.e., attending to and
accurately perceiving the behavior) and retention (i.e., symbolic processing of the modeled behavior) are cognitive processes. Therefore,
Answer A is correct.
Answer B: Although Bandura acknowledges that social approval may have a reinforcing effect on a behavior, observation of new behavior is the
primary focus of social learning theory.
Answer C: This is the opposite of what is true. Bandura proposed that reinforcement is more important for performance than learning.
Answer D: Exploring internalized S-R connections is not a part of Bandura's social learning theory. The focus of social learning theory is on the
four intervening variables between stimuli and response that are identi�ed above.

questions.question: According to Albert Ellis, maladaptive behavior is caused primarily by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The basic premise of Ellis's rational-emotive behavior therapy (REBT) is that maladaptive behaviors and emotions are the result of irrational
thoughts and beliefs. Thus, the primary goal of REBT is to replace the client's irrational thoughts and beliefs with more rational, adaptive ones,
which will ultimately reduce the occurrence of maladaptive behavior. Knowing that Ellis's approach is classi�ed as a type of cognitive-
behavioral therapy would have helped you identify the correct response to this question.
Answer A: Learned helplessness, discovered by Martin Seligman and Steven F. Maier, is the phenomenon that occurs when an individual is
consistently exposed to an aversive experience outside of their control and ultimately stops trying to change their circumstances, even when
opportunities to do so are presented.
Answer B: In gestalt therapy, the term "boundary disturbance" is used to describe an individual's di�culty with differentiating one's self from
their environment. Good boundaries are viewed as critical for health and survival. Con�uence occurs when the separation between self and
others is unidenti�able, and isolation occurs when the boundary between self and others is impermeable.
Answer C: Response-contingent reinforcement is a principle outlined in behavior therapy used to conceptualize the development of depression:
when the degree of positive reinforcement experienced in response to healthy behaviors decreases, decreased behavioral activation and
increased depressive symptoms occur.

questions.question: Elmo, age 5, has learned that if he has a tantrum at mealtime whenever his parents want him to eat food he doesn't like, his parents will let him eat something else instead so that he will stop crying. In this situation, the parents' behavior (letting Elmo eat something other than the disliked food) is being maintained by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Escape conditioning is a type of negative reinforcement (i.e., operant conditioning) that occurs when a person's behavior is maintained
because it allows the person to escape an undesirable stimulus. In this situation, the parents' choice to let Elmo eat something other than the
disliked food is negatively reinforced because it results in termination of his tantrum.
Answer B: Avoidance conditioning is another type of negative reinforcement that occurs when a cue signals that the undesirable stimulus is
about to begin. In this case, the undesirable stimulus can be avoided entirely if the individual performs the appropriate (i.e., reinforced) behavior
in response to the cue.
Answer C: Stimulus discrimination, a classical conditioning concept, occurs when a conditioned response occurs only in response to a speci�c
conditioned stimulus and not in response to other stimuli.
Answer D: In stimulus generalization (also a concept in classical conditioning), the individual responds with a conditioned response to stimuli
that are similar to the original conditioned stimulus.

questions.question: In Pavlov's research with animals, he found that dogs began to salivate in response to a tone after the tone had been presented repeatedly with meat powder. In this situation, the tone was:
questions.explanation:
In classical conditioning, an unconditioned stimulus (US) naturally elicits an unconditioned response (UR). A conditioned stimulus (CS) elicits a
conditioned response (CR) after it has been repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus (US). In Pavlov's studies, the tone was a
conditioned stimulus (CS) because it elicited salivation (the CR) only as the result of being paired with the meat powder (the US) that naturally
elicited salivation (the UR).
Answer B: The unconditioned stimulus (US) elicits a response without any learning trials (i.e., pairing with other stimuli). In this situation, the US
is the meat powder.
Answer C: In operant conditioning, primary reinforcers are reinforcers that are inherently reinforcing, such as food or water.
Answer D: In operant conditioning, secondary reinforcers are reinforcers that have been conditioned to be reinforcing as a result of being paired
with primary reinforcers. For example, tokens in a token economy, money, or grades in school are secondary reinforcers because they are
associated with primary reinforcers (e.g., can be used to buy food, result in the experience of pleasure).

questions.question: Samuel, age 43, says, "Even though I've just been given a bonus at work, I feel like I'm about to be �red." As de�ned by Aaron Beck, Samuel is exhibiting which of the following cognitive distortions?
questions.explanation:
As de�ned by Beck, "arbitrary inference" involves drawing a conclusion that is made in the absence of supporting evidence or in the presence of
contradictory evidence. That de�nition �ts this situation.
Answer A: "Musturbatory thinking" is a term used by Ellis that refers to a belief that certain conditions must be met in order for an individual to
be happy—for example "I must be liked by everyone, and if not, I'm a terrible person."
Answer B: "Polarized," or dichotomous, thinking involves seeing things as either black or white, with few to no shades of gray, consistent with
the "all-or-none" principle.
Answer C: "Personalization" involves mistakenly viewing oneself as the cause of a negative event even if it was entirely out of one's control.

questions.question: Research on the serial position effect provides support for the distinction between:
questions.explanation:
The "serial position effect" refers to the tendency to recall items at the beginning and end of a list better than items in the middle of the list,
especially when recall occurs immediately after rehearsing the list. One explanation for the serial position effect is that items in the beginning
of the list have been stored in long-term memory, while those in the end of the list are still present in short-term memory.
Answer A: Iconic (visual) and echoic (auditory) memory are both types of sensory memory, a brief memory that allows sensory information to
be retained long enough for it to be recognized prior to transfer of important details into short-term memory.
Answer B: Parallel processing is the brain's ability to take in and process multiple sources of information at once. For example, when one sees
a stop sign, they do not �rst see the shape, then the color, then the words; instead, they process them all simultaneously. Distributed
processing postulates multiple memory systems into which information is processed in a step-by-step manner (e.g., sensory, then short-term,
then long-term).
Answer D: Proactive interference is when previously learned information or older memories interfere with learning new information or retrieving
newer memories (e.g., di�culty learning or recalling a friend's phone number after having previously learned the old number). Retroactive
interference is when new information interferes with one's ability to recall older memories or previously learned information (e.g., a piano player
learns to play a new song and then has di�culty recalling how to play an old song).

questions.question: When using the Premack principle to modify a behavior, the reinforcer is:

options.D: a stimulus that naturally elicits the desired behavior.

questions.explanation:
The Premack principle is a type of positive reinforcement in which a high-frequency behavior is used as the reinforcer to increase the frequency
of a low-frequency, less desired behavior. It is also known as "Grandma's Rule" (e.g., "you can go out and play [a highly desired behavior] once
you've cleaned your room [a less desired behavior]").
Answer A: The reinforcer (i.e., the high-frequency, desirable behavior) must be applied consistently.
Answer B: The reinforcer is a naturally reinforcing behavior, not conditioned.
Answer D: The reinforcer only elicits the desired behavior because it is contingent upon the desired behavior being performed (e.g., a student
studies for an hour because only then are they permitted to play video games).

questions.question: A behavior therapist working with a child who bites her nails sets a timer so that it rings every 5 minutes. The child is then given a reward for every 5-minute period that she doesn't bite her nails. The therapist is using which of the following techniques?
questions.explanation:
The child is being reinforced for every 5-minute period during which she engages in behaviors other than biting her nails. Differential
reinforcement is when non-target behaviors are reinforced but the target behavior is not.
Answer B: Response cost is a punishment procedure that involves withdrawing a conditioned reinforcer following occurrence of a target
behavior to decrease the target behavior.
Answer C: Overcorrection is used to reduce undesirable behaviors. It involves having the individual engage in repetition of appropriate
behaviors in response to occurrence of the undesirable behavior (i.e., returning the environment to its previous condition).
Answer D: When using the Premack principle, a high-frequency behavior is used as a reinforcer for a low-frequency behavior to increase the
occurrence of the low-frequency behavior.

questions.question: John Watson found that after Little Albert had been classically conditioned to respond with fear to a white rat, the child also responded with fear to other white furry objects. Little Albert's reaction to other white furry objects was the result of:
questions.explanation:
Stimulus generalization occurs when an individual responds with a conditioned response to stimuli that are similar to the original conditioned
stimulus. Little Albert's response (fear) to a speci�c conditioned stimulus (the white rat) generalized to similar stimuli (other white furry
objects).
Answer A: Higher-order conditioning is a classical conditioning technique in which a neutral stimulus elicits a conditioned response as a result
of its pairing with a conditioned stimulus. In Little Albert's situation, other white furry objects were not "paired with" the white rat.
Answer B: Negative transfer occurs when previous learning interferes with new learning.
Answer C: Pseudoconditioning occurs when a conditioned response occurs following repeated exposure to the unconditioned stimulus only
(i.e., when the neutral stimulus is not paired with the unconditioned stimulus but its presentation elicits a response similar to the conditioned
response). For example, Wickens & Wickens (1940) found that a mild shock (US) and a buzzer (NS) both elicited the response of foot
withdrawal after early training had involved presenting the mild shock repeatedly on its own without pairing with the buzzer.

questions.question: Dismantling studies have found evidence that which of the following principles is attributable to the effectiveness of systematic desensitization as a treatment for anxiety?
questions.explanation:
Systematic desensitization was developed as an application of reciprocal inhibition (counterconditioning). However, research using the
dismantling strategy suggests that reciprocal inhibition is not the essential component. Instead, the results of this research has led researchers
to conclude that repeated exposure to feared stimuli leads to the extinction of the undesirable anxiety response and is responsible for the
bene�ts of systematic desensitization. (For a description of the dismantling strategy, see the Learning Theory chapter of the written study
materials.)
Answer A: Escape conditioning is a form of aversive conditioning in which a subject responds to the presentation of an aversive/unpleasant
stimulus by engaging in a behavior to escape that stimulus and the alternative behavior is thus reinforced. It does not allow for continued
exposure to the anxiety trigger as is necessary in systematic desensitization.
Answer C: Satiation is an operant conditioning term. It occurs when the frequency of a reinforced behavior decreases despite the continued
presence of the reinforcer due to continued contact with the reinforcer to the point of excess and subsequent reduction of the effectiveness of
the reinforcer.
Answer D: Higher-order conditioning is a classical conditioning technique in which a neutral stimulus elicits a conditioned response as a result
of its pairing with a conditioned stimulus and is not related to systematic desensitization.

questions.question: The technique known as "stress inoculation training" consists of three overlapping phases. These are:

options.C: initiation of treatment, primary treatment/rehabilitation, and aftercare.
options.D: conceptualization/education, skill acquisition and rehearsal, and application and follow through.

questions.explanation:
Stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum & Jaremko, 1982) was designed to help people deal with stressful events by increasing their coping
skills. It is a cognitive-behavioral technique that consists of the three phases listed in this response.
Answer A: These phases are common in re�ective practices.
Answer B: These components are 3 of the 5 major components of functional family therapy.
Answer C: These are common components of many methods for treating substance use and addiction.

questions.question: When using a continuous schedule of reinforcement to increase the occurrence of a desirable behavior, you would be most concerned about which of the following?
questions.explanation:
A continuous schedule of reinforcement involves reinforcing the individual every time they emit the target response. Satiation occurs when a
reinforcer loses its reinforcing value because the organism has become satis�ed (satiated). It is a potential problem when using positive
reinforcement, especially when the reinforcer is a primary reinforcer and is delivered on a continuous schedule.
Answer B: In the context of learning theory, sensitization has at least two meanings: it refers to either the initial increase in responsiveness to a
stimulus when it is presented repeatedly or to the increase in responsiveness to a stimulus that occurs after exposure to a very intense or
irritating stimulus.
Answer C: Experimental neurosis occurs in classical conditioning when the organism is required to discriminate between very similar stimuli.
Answer D: Spontaneous recovery refers to the return of a conditioned response following the apparent extinction of that response.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes elaborative rehearsal?

options.C: Practicing a new skill past the point of mastery

questions.explanation:
Researchers interested in memory distinguish between two types of rehearsal: elaborative and maintenance. Elaborative rehearsal involves
making new information meaningful in order to enhance its retention and retrieval. Relating new information to previously acquired information
is one type of elaborative rehearsal.
Answer B: This sounds more like maintenance rehearsal, which involves the rote repetition of information.
Answer C: This response describes "overlearning."
Answer D: This response describes the "thinking aloud method," not elaborative rehearsal.

questions.question: The "law of effect" was proposed by:
questions.explanation:
According to the law of effect, a response that is followed by a "satisfying state of affairs" is more likely to be repeated. Thorndike's
experiments with cats in puzzle boxes established a connection between the consequences of a behavior and the likelihood that the behavior
will be repeated, and he referred to this connection as the "law of effect."
Answer A: Tolman is associated with cognitive maps and research with rats that led to his identi�cation of "latent learning."
Answer C: Watson used Pavlovian (classical) conditioning to explain the development of fear responses.
Answer D: Bandura is most associated with social (observational) learning theory.

questions.question: Children living in a residential facility are rewarded with a speci�c number of tokens each time they perform desirable behaviors but must return a certain number of tokens when they engage in undesirable behaviors. The latter technique (returning tokens) exempli�es which of the following?
questions.explanation:
This question is asking which technique involves removing a stimulus following a behavior in order to reduce or eliminate that behavior.
Response cost is used to eliminate an undesirable behavior and involves imposing a penalty or �ne (i.e., removing a speci�c stimulus)
whenever the undesirable behavior occurs. Response cost is an application of negative punishment. Note that, for the exam, you want to be
familiar with all four techniques listed in the answers to this question. These techniques are described in greater detail in the Learning Theory
chapter of the written study materials.
Answer A: Negative reinforcement involves removing a stimulus following a behavior, but its goal is to increase the behavior, not to decrease it.
Answer C: The Premack principle involves using a high-frequency behavior as a reinforcer for a low-frequency behavior in order to increase the
low-frequency behavior.
Answer D: Differential reinforcement is used to decrease an undesirable behavior by reinforcing alternative behaviors. It does not involve
removing a speci�c stimulus (e.g., tokens) following the undesirable behavior, which is what is occurring in the situation described in this
question.

questions.question: The process of gradually removing a prompt until it is no longer provided is referred to as:
questions.explanation:
The process of gradually eliminating prompts is referred to as "fading."
Answer A: Extinction refers to the removal of an unconditioned stimulus and presenting the conditioned stimulus alone (classical conditioning)
or to removing a reinforcer that has been maintaining a behavior (operant conditioning).
Answer B: Shaping involves reinforcing successive approximations of the desired behavior (i.e., any behavior leading to the development of the
target behavior is rewarded).
Answer D: Thinning is the process of gradually reducing the frequency of reinforcement (i.e., switching from a continuous to an intermittent
schedule of reinforcement).

questions.question: Findings from studies comparing participants' ability to recall a list of words they had memorized based on whether or not they were allowed to sleep following memorization provide support for which of the following theories?
questions.explanation:
Interference theory proposes that accurate memory recall is impaired due to interference from other, similar memories. The research referred
to in this question found that participants who slept remembered more than those who stayed awake. The results of this research suggest that
forgetting is not due simply to the passage of time but, instead, to the events that follow learning. In other words, memory loss is due to the
interference of other events.
Answer A: Trace decay theory predicts that forgetting is due to the passage of time. If this theory were correct, participants who did not sleep
would have exhibited similar levels of recall compared to those who did sleep.
Answer C: Freud proposed that motivated forgetting is due to the repression of unconscious desires.
Answer D: Retrieval failure theory predicts that memory loss is due to an inability to retrieve information from long-term memory, as opposed to
failure to store information.

questions.question: ____________ used chimpanzees as his research subjects in studies designed to investigate the role of cognition in learning.
questions.explanation:
All of the individuals listed in the answer options conducted studies on learning. However, Kohler was the only one to use chimpanzees as his
research subjects. Kohler's work with chimpanzees led to his description of insight learning.
Answer A: Tolman's research with rats led to his identi�cation of "latent learning."
Answer B: Ebbinghaus acted as his own subject in research on forgetting.
Answer C: Thorndike's experiments with cats in puzzle boxes led to the formulation of the "law of effect."

questions.question: A friend describes what the hot fudge sundae you are eating reminds him of in the most disgusting terms he can call to mind just as you begin to eat. He does this several times until you can no longer continue eating the sundae because it makes you feel sick. This situation has the closest resemblance to which of the following techniques?
questions.explanation:
This situation is most like covert sensitization, a type of aversive counterconditioning in which an undesirable behavior is paired with an
unpleasant image. The goal of covert sensitization is to change the desirable response that occurs in response to a conditioned stimulus (CS)
to an undesirable response in order to eliminate a behavior. As the result of pairing an imagined aversive scene with a sundae, eating a sundae
has become unpleasant, and subsequently, "sundae-eating behavior" will be avoided or eliminated. The imagined aversive scene is the
unconditioned stimulus (US), the sundae is the conditioned stimulus (CS), and the resulting avoidance behavior is both the unconditioned and
conditioned response (UR/CR).
Answer A: This situation is not similar to operant shaping, which uses reinforcement of successive approximations of a desired behavior to
increase or establish that behavior.
Answer B: This situation is not similar to prompting and fading. Prompting (e.g., giving verbal instructions, giving physical guidance, or using
nonverbal cues) is used to facilitate the acquisition of a new behavior. Fading is the gradual removal of prompts.
Answer C: This situation is not similar to paradoxical intention, which involves imagining an exaggerated version of conditions surrounding a
fear in order to eliminate the fear.

questions.question: The phenomenon known as "blocking" will occur in which of the following circumstances?

options.A: The CS is presented prior to the US until a CR is established; then the CS and a new neutral stimulus are presented together several times prior to the US.
options.B: The CS is presented prior to the US until a CR is established; then the CS is presented several times with a new neutral stimulus until the CR is extinguished.
options.C: The CS is presented prior to the US until a CR is established; then a new neutral stimulus is presented prior to the CS.
options.D: The CS is presented prior to the US until a CR is established; then a new neutral stimulus is presented after the CS.

questions.explanation:
Blocking occurs when a conditioned stimulus (CS) blocks a second neutral stimulus from becoming a CS. The �rst step to blocking is
establishing an association between the CS and the unconditioned stimulus (US). Then, a new neutral stimulus is presented in conjunction with
the CS prior to presenting the US. When this sequence is followed, the new neutral stimulus provides redundant information because the
occurrence of the US was fully predicted by the already-conditioned response (the CS) alone. Consequently, the neutral stimulus does not
become associated with the US and does not produce a conditioned response (CR). This is the process described in Answer A.
Answer B: The CR does not occur in response to the neutral stimulus when presented alone, but it does continue to occur in response to the
original CS. Therefore, the CR is not extinguished.
Answer C: In blocking, the CS and the new neutral stimulus are presented at the same time, prior to the US.
Answer D: The new neutral stimulus must be presented together with the CS and prior to the US.

questions.question: Children experiencing peer rejection versus children subject to peer neglect experience which trajectory when changing schools?

options.A: School change has no effect on the status of rejected children but may have bene�cial effects on the peer status of neglected children.
options.B: School change has no effect on the peer status of neglected children but may have bene�cial effects on the peer status of rejected children.
options.C: School change is likely to have no effect on the peer status of either rejected or neglected children.
options.D: School change is likely to have bene�cial effects on the peer status of both rejected and neglected children.

questions.explanation:
Coie and Kupersmidt showed that peer rejection tends to be stable across social transitions and is maintained in novel social groups, while
those that are peer neglected may improve relations in the new setting (Coie, John D., and Kupersmidt, Janis B, "A Behavioral Analysis of
Emerging Social Status in Boys' Groups," Child Development, 1983, 54, 1400-1416).
Answer B: As noted above, Coie and Kupersmidt's data show that those who have experienced peer rejection do not typically improve social
relations in new settings, in contrast to students who have been peer neglected.
Answer C: As noted above, Coie and Kupersmidt's �ndings do show a difference in the social transitions between peer rejected and peer
neglected students.
Answer D: As noted above, the bene�cial effect shown by Coie and Kupersmidt is only observed in peer neglected students.

questions.question: Aging causes what change in the focal point of the eye?

options.A: The near focal point will move away from the eyes.
options.B: The near focal point will move closer to our eyes.
options.C: The near focal point will remain the same, but the distant focal point will move away from our eyes.
options.D: The near focal point will remain the same, but the distant focal point will move closer to our eyes.

questions.explanation:
The process of accommodation, de�ned by the near and far focal point, is changed by the hardening of the visual lens with age. The near focal
point moves farther away.
Answer B: In aging, the near focal point moves farther away.
Answer C: In aging, the near focal point moves farther away with no change in the distant focal point.
Answer D: In aging, the near focal point moves farther away while the distant focal point remains the same.

questions.question: Current theories consider "emotional contagion" to be the earliest manifestation of empathy development. This behavior emerges:

options.B: between two and four months of age.
options.C: at about six months of age.
options.D: at about one year of age.

questions.explanation:
Emotional contagion refers to the tendency of babies to cry at the sound of another infant's cries. This occurs in infants as young as two days
old and is considered by experts to be the �rst sign of empathy.
Answers B, C, and D: Emotional contagion occurs in the earliest days of infancy.

questions.question: The intellectual disability associated with PKU is preventable with:
questions.explanation:
PKU (phenylketonuria) involves an inability to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine. Intellectual disability and other symptoms of PKU can
be reduced or eliminated by a diet low in phenylalanine beginning at birth.
Answer A: PKU is a recessive gene disorder that is not related to environmental toxins.
Answer B: PKU is not addressed with blood transfusions.
Answer D: Antibiotics are not used with PKU, as it is not due to infection.

questions.question: Independent, self-con�dent adolescents, according to Baumrind and colleagues (1991), are most likely to have parents who are:
questions.explanation:
Baumrind and her colleagues distinguish between authoritarian, authoritative, permissive, and rejecting-neglecting parents. The authoritative
style is most likely to produce independent, self-con�dent children and adolescents. Authoritative parents combine rational control with
warmth, receptivity, and the encouragement of independence. It's very likely that you'll encounter a question on these styles on the exam, so be
familiar with their characteristics and effects, which are described in the written study materials.
Answer B: Authoritarian parents impose absolute standards of control and stress obedience, and they are willing to use force to obtain
compliance. Their children tend to be insecure, anxious, and dependent and display a limited sense of responsibility.
Answer C: Permissive parents provide their children with few controls or demands and display moderate levels of warmth. Their children exhibit
little self-reliance, exploratory behavior, or self-control.
Answer D:"Traditional" is not a parenting style identi�ed by Baumrind.

questions.question: Babbling ordinarily begins at about 4 to 5 months of age and initially includes:

options.B: phonemes from the child's native language only.
options.D: morphemes that the child has heard most frequently.

questions.explanation:
Babbling involves the repetition of vowel and consonant sounds—e.g., bi-bi-bi and da-da-da. These are simple units of sound without meaning,
de�nitive of a phoneme.
Answer B: Babbling initially consists of phonemes from all languages. By about 9 months, it narrows to include the sounds of the child's native
language only.
Answer C: A morpheme is distinguished by having meaning. Babbling consists of sounds without meaning.
Answer D: A morpheme is distinguished by having meaning. Babbling consists of sounds without meaning.

questions.question: Children obey rules during the second stage of Kohlberg's preconventional level of moral development, because:

options.A: they feel they have a personal duty to uphold rules and laws.
options.C: doing so helps them avoid punishment.
options.D: doing so helps them satisfy their personal needs.

questions.explanation:
Kohlberg's theory of moral development consists of three levels, with each level including two stages. Instrumental hedonism is the second
stage of the preconventional level. Children in this stage consider the correct action to be the one that best satis�es their own personal needs.
Kohlberg illustrates this stage with the example of a 10-year-old boy's reply to what it means to be a good son: "Be good to your father, and he
will be good to you."
Answer A: This is characteristic of the second stage of Kohlberg's conventional, not preconventional, level.
Answer B: This doesn't describe the second stage of the preconventional level.
Answer C: This is characteristic of the �rst stage of the preconventional level (punishment and obedience stage). For the exam, you want to be
familiar with the characteristics of the six stages, which are described in the Lifespan Development chapter of the written study materials.

questions.question: A 16-month-old child who calls her pet cat "kitty" sees a dog for the �rst time and calls it "kitty." The child is displaying ____________ in Piaget's theory of cognitive development.
questions.explanation:
Piaget distinguished between two complementary processes in cognitive development: assimilation and accommodation. Assimilation
involves incorporating new knowledge into existing cognitive structures or schemes. The child in the question doesn't know what a dog is and
is incorporating it into her existing "kitty" scheme.
Answer B: Accommodation involves modifying an existing scheme or creating a new one.
Answer C: Piaget did not use the term "categorization" to describe the incorporation of new knowledge into an existing cognitive scheme.
Answer D: Centration is a limitation of the preoperational stage and refers to the tendency to focus on the most salient aspect of an object.

questions.question: Children's successful adjustment to the divorce of their parents is most related to:

options.A: the frequency of contact with the noncustodial parent.
options.B: the quality of the parent–child relationships prior to the divorce.
options.C: the child's ability to understand the cause(s) of the divorce.
options.D: the degree of post-divorce con�ict between the parents.

questions.explanation:
The frequency and severity of post-divorce con�ict between the parents has most consistently been linked to children's adjustment. Some
experts argue that this factor, rather than divorce, determines post-divorce adjustment problems in children.
Answers A, B, and C: A number of child and parent factors have been linked to children's adjustment to the divorce of their parents, but Answer
D is the strongest predictor.

questions.question: Thomas and Chess's "goodness-of-�t" model (1977) predicts that maladjustment in children is due to:

options.A: a mismatch between the child's basic temperament and their parents' child rearing practices.
options.B: a mismatch between the child's attachment behaviors and their parents' response to those behaviors.
options.C: inconsistencies in the parenting styles of the child's caregivers.
options.D: inconsistencies in the child's sense of self and the feedback the child receives from caregivers about their behavior.

questions.explanation:
Thomas and Chess concluded that it is not the child's early temperament that predicts future adjustment, but the match between the child's
temperament and their caregivers' child rearing practices.
Answer B: Thomas and Chess studied temperament, not attachment.
Answer C: Thomas and Chess studied temperament, not parenting style.
Answer D: Thomas and Chess studied temperament, not self-esteem.

questions.question: Stranger anxiety begins in most children at about _____ months of age.
questions.explanation:
Stranger anxiety involves anxious, fearful responses in the presence of a stranger, especially when a caregiver is not present. Most experts
agree that it begins during the second half of the �rst year, although there may be disagreement as to the exact age of onset.
Answers A, B, and D: Stranger anxiety begins in most children at about 8 to 10 months of age.

questions.question: Alice, age 14, is certain that everyone is looking at her because she has a large blemish in the middle of her forehead. Alice's belief, according to Elkind (1967), is a manifestation of:
questions.explanation:
Elkind proposed that adolescents experience a renewed egocentrism that is manifested in several ways (1967). He used the term "imaginary
audience" to describe the adolescent's belief that they are the focus of everyone's attention.
Answer A: Self-conscious emotions include shame, embarrassment, and pride; these are not relevant to Elkind's explanation for Alice's
behavior.
Answer B: The personal fable is one manifestation of adolescent egocentrism but does not describe Alice's concern. It refers to the belief that
one is special and unique and not subject to the same dangers as other people are.
Answer C: Social referencing refers to relying on the emotional response of another person to decide how to respond in an ambiguous
situation.

questions.question: Interactions between elements of the microsystem (e.g., between the family and the school) are part of the ____________ in Bronfenbrenner's model (2004).
questions.explanation:
Bronfenbrenner's ecological model distinguishes between �ve layers (levels) that in�uence a child's development: microsystem, mesosystem,
exosystem, macrosystem, and chronosystem. The mesosystem is the second layer and consists of interactions between components of the
microsystem (e.g., the parents' involvement in the child's school experiences and interactions between the child's church and community).
Answer B: The exosystem consists of elements in the social setting that indirectly affect the child's development (e.g., the parents' jobs).
Answer C: The macrosystem is the outermost layer and includes the values, laws, customs, etc. of the child's culture.
Answer D: The endosystem is not one of the levels identi�ed by Bronfenbrenner.

questions.question: The age range of Erikson's ____________ stage of psychosocial development corresponds to Freud's phallic stage.
questions.explanation:
Erikson's initiative vs. guilt stage is characteristic of children aged 3 to 6 years, which corresponds to Freud's phallic stage.
Answer A: The industry vs. inferiority stage is characteristic of children aged 6 to 11 years and corresponds to Freud's latency stage.
Answer B: The autonomy vs. shame and doubt stage occurs between the ages of 1 and 3 years and corresponds to Freud's anal stage.
Answer C: The basic trust vs. mistrust stage occurs from birth to 1 year of age and corresponds to Freud's oral stage. Erikson's psychosocial
theory proposes that personality development occurs throughout the lifespan and involves eight stages. For the exam, be familiar with the
names of the stages and the ages at which they occur.

questions.question: A child with an insecure/avoidant pattern of attachment:

options.A: is very distressed when separated from their mother and continues to be highly anxious when she returns.
options.B: is more anxious when their mother is present than absent and resists contact with her when she returns following separation.
options.C: is very distressed when separated from their mother but pulls away from her when she returns.
options.D: shows little distress when separated from their mother and turns away from her when she returns.

questions.explanation:
In Ainsworth's "strange situation," insecure/avoidant children are uninterested in exploration, show little distress when separated from their
mothers, and avoid her when she returns.
Answer A: This does not describe any of the typical patterns in the "strange situation."
Answer B: This describes the pattern of disorganized/disoriented attachment.
Answer C: This describes the pattern of insecure/ambivalent attachment. The four attachment patterns described by Ainsworth and her
colleagues (secure, insecure/ambivalent, insecure/avoidant, and disorganized/disoriented) are described in the Lifespan Development chapter
of the written study materials. You'll want to become familiar with the characteristics associated with each pattern because you're likely to
encounter a question similar to this one on the exam.

questions.question: Konrad Lorenz's research on "imprinting" (1957) led to the search for ____________ in human infants.

options.B: a biological explanation for language acquisition
options.C: a sensitive period for social referencing
options.D: a biological mechanism for recognition memory

questions.explanation:
Imprinting refers to the bond that develops during a critical period following birth in some non-human species. The ethologist Lorenz found that
geese bonded to the �rst moving object they encounter during the �rst few days following birth. His research led to a search for a similar
"critical period" for attachment in human infants.
Answer B: Lorenz's research on imprinting does not relate to language acquisition.
Answer C: The term "sensitive period" is relevant, but Lorenz's research did not lead to studies on social referencing.
Answer D: Lorenz's research on imprinting does not relate to cognition.

questions.question: ____________ is a key contributor to aggressive behavior in children, according to Gerald Patterson and his colleagues (1992).

options.C: The strength of the parent–child attachment

questions.explanation:
The social learning approach of Patterson and his colleagues focuses on the family factors that contribute to aggressiveness in children.
Patterson et al.'s "coercive family interaction model" attributes aggression in children primarily to interactions between parents and their
children, especially interactions involving the parents' child rearing behaviors.
Answer A: The child's intelligence was not a factor identi�ed by Patterson et al.'s research.
Answer B: The child's personality was not a factor identi�ed by Patterson et al.'s research.
Answer C: Although this answer refers to a family factor, attachment patterns are not the focus of this research.

questions.question: The ____________ is the least developed area of the brain at birth.
questions.explanation:
