The higher centers of the brain are the most complex and develop last. The cerebral cortex, which is responsible for higher-level cognitive skills,
complex motor behaviors, language, and spatial skills, is almost completely undeveloped at birth.
Answer A: The brain stem, which controls life-maintaining functions, is the lowest brain level and is present at birth.
Answer C: The limbic system, in the mid-brain, is mostly developed at birth.
Answer D: Although recent studies have shown continued cerebellar development during childhood, the cerebellum, which primarily controls
motor function, is more developed at birth than the cerebral cortex.

questions.question: Most babies say their �rst words at about _____ months of age.
questions.explanation:
For the exam, be familiar with the language milestones of early childhood that are described in the Lifespan Development chapter of the written
study materials. Most infants say their �rst recognizable word at 12 months of age.
Answers A, B, and D: Most babies say their �rst words at about 12 months of age.

questions.question: Children begin to deliberately and regularly use rehearsal, elaboration, and organization as memory strategies by _____ years of age.
questions.explanation:
The research has shown that the deliberate and consistent use of the memory strategies listed in the question begins at about 9 to 10 years of
age.
Answer A: The consistent and deliberate use of memory strategies does not occur until age 9 or 10.
Answer B: Preschoolers sometimes use memory strategies, but they do so in non-deliberate and often ineffective ways. In addition, children of
this age can be taught to use memory strategies for a speci�c task but do not apply them to new tasks.
Answer D: The use of these strategies continues to be "�ne-tuned" during adolescence, but their use begins earlier.

questions.question: ____________ involves intellectual disability and extreme obesity and is caused by a chromosomal deletion.
questions.explanation:
Approximately 1 in 200 babies is born with a chromosomal abnormality. Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by a chromosomal deletion, which
occurs when part of a chromosome is missing.
Answer A: Down syndrome is attributable to the presence of an extra chromosome, not a deleted chromosome.
Answer B: Turner syndrome is caused by the absence of a chromosome. It occurs only in females and involves the absence of one X
chromosome.
Answer C: Klinefelter syndrome occurs in males and is due to the presence of two or more X chromosomes and a single Y chromosome.

questions.question: The rooting re�ex occurs when:

options.C: the newborn hears their caregiver's voice.
options.D: the newborn hears an unexpected loud noise.

questions.explanation:
Re�exes are unlearned responses to particular stimuli in the environment. The rooting re�ex occurs when the baby turns their head in the
direction of a touch or stroke on their cheek.
Answer B: This describes the Babinski re�ex.
Answer C: This does not describe the rooting re�ex.
Answer D: This describes the Moro (startle) re�ex.

questions.question: Auditory localization in children:

options.A: is fully developed by 2 or 3 months of age.
options.B: does not begin to develop until the 8th or 9th month.
options.C: has fully developed by about the end of the �rst year.
options.D: shows a burst in development during the preschool years.

questions.explanation:
Auditory localization refers to the ability to orient toward the direction of a sound (i.e., to turn one's head toward the sound). This ability is not
consistently established until about 1 year.
Answer A: Infants exhibit some auditory localization during the �rst month of life, but between two and four months, there seems to be a loss
of this ability. At four months, the ability returns, and by one year, it is almost completely established.
Answer B: As noted above, this ability is noted for a brief period in early infancy, so it is not correct to say it begins at 8 months.
Answer D: Preschool is not a relevant time frame for this ability.

questions.question: Factors that predict adolescent drug use in Shedler and Block's longitudinal studies (1990) include:

options.B: lack of information about the effects of drugs.

questions.explanation:
This study of preschool to age 18 found that social maladjustment predates frequent drug use in adolescence.
Answer A: There is no evidence that peer pressure determines adolescent drug use.
Answer B: Lack of information is not a factor in adolescent drug use.
Answer D: Experimentation with drugs is common in adolescence and does not distinguish the teens that progress to frequent drug use.

questions.question: Most infants take their �rst steps with support at about:
questions.explanation:
Developmental motor ability at 9–10 months normally includes taking steps while holding onto furniture.
Answer A: Most children are not taking steps prior to 9 months.
Answer C: Walking without support typically occurs at 12–13 months.
Answer D: 15–16 months is well beyond the expected age for needing support to walk.

questions.question: Considering the Rosenthal effect, students described to teachers as "academic successes" are likely to:

options.A: achieve more than the other students by the end of the school year.
options.B: be mistreated by fellow students who are jealous of their status.
options.C: exhibit academic anxiety due to pressure from the teacher.
options.D: be no different from the other students at the end of the school year.

questions.explanation:
The Rosenthal Effect states that creating expectations for achievement has a self-ful�lling effect.
Answer B: Advising teachers that some students are achievers does not necessarily result in bullying.
Answer C: The Rosenthal Effect has not been linked to anxiety.
Answer D: Students perform better than peers in this situation.

questions.question: Which of the following is true characteristic of sleeping patterns of older adults?
questions.explanation:
The circadian clock advances as we age, which results in an advanced sleep phase. This means that individuals becomes somnolent earlier in
the evening and wake up earlier in the morning.
Answer A: Advanced age is associated with decreases in REM (not increases) and slow-wave sleep, which is a combination of Stage 3 and
Stage 4 sleep.
Answer B: A lack of sleep at night is accompanied by increased somnolence during the day.
Answer D: A delayed sleep phase occurs when a person's sleep is delayed by two hours or more beyond what is a conventional bedtime.

questions.question: Hypothyroidism is associated with:

options.B: emotional lability, unrealistic fears and doubts, and impaired concentration.
options.C: agitated paranoia, confusion, hallucinations, and delusions.
options.D: unprovoked anger, episodic confusion, and lethargy or fatigue.

questions.explanation:
Depression accompanied by symptoms indicative of bradyphrenia may serve as evidence of untreated hypothyroidism.
Answer B: These symptoms are indicative of hyperthyroidism.
Answer C: These symptoms are indicative of hyperparathyroidism.
Answer D: This symptom presentation is typical for hypoglycemia.

questions.question: A patient is shown a �ower in her left visual �eld, and touches it with her left hand. She is then shown the �ower in her right visual �eld and touches it with her right hand. This suggests that the woman has experienced damage to which of the following areas of her brain?
questions.explanation:
Research on "split-brain" patients has found that severing the corpus callosum limits the amount of information that can be transferred from
one hemisphere to the other.
Answer A: Although the hippocampus is involved with memory, damage to the hippocampus will not necessarily result in the behavior
described in this question.
Answer B: The cerebellum governs coordinated movements.
Answer D: The amygdala is part of the limbic system and involved in the regulation of emotions.

questions.question: The ____________ is a key structure in the mediation of conditioned fear.
questions.explanation:
Neurons in the amygdala are responsible for the formation of conditioned fear memory and the expression of conditioned fear response.
Answer A: The hippocampus is critical for storing memories for individual events.
Answer B: The main function of the thalamus is to relay motor and sensory signals to the cerebral cortex.
Answer D: The reticular formation plays a central role in states of consciousness like alertness and sleep.

questions.question: When an individual sustains damage to the frontal lobe, which of the following is least likely to occur?

options.A: loss of movement in various parts of the body

questions.explanation:
Di�culty with differentiating between right and left is a hallmark symptom of Gerstmann syndrome and typically results from damage to the
left parietal lobe.
Answer A: Both the pre-motor and motor areas are located in the frontal lobe. The pre-motor area is responsible for planning
movement and the motor area is responsible for initiating voluntary muscle movement, so damage to the frontal lobe could result in
di�culty with carrying out movement.
Answer B: The prefrontal cortex, responsible for executive functioning and many higher order cognitive processes, allows individuals
to shift their attention, inhibit impulses, and engage in cognitive �exibility. When there is damage to this area, an individual may
experience repetitive speech, behavior, or thoughts, also known as perseveration.
Answer C: Broca’s area, located in the left frontal lobe, is responsible for the muscles that produce speech. Damage to this area can
result in signi�cant di�culty with articulation and speech production even though the individual may understand language and are
aware of what they want to say.

questions.question: What part of the brain plays a role in the etiology of seasonal affective disorder (SAD)?
questions.explanation:
The suprachiasmatic nucleus mediates sleep cycles, wake cycles, and circadian rhythms, all of which are affected in seasonal affective
disorder.
Answer A: The red nucleus is a midbrain structure that is involved in motor coordination.
Answer C: The tectum is part of the midbrain and is involved in auditory and visual processing.
Answer D: The striatum is part of the basal ganglia and is involved in movement and cognitive processing.

questions.question: Huntington's disease is a/an:
questions.explanation:
Autosomal dominant disorders occur when only one defective copy of an autosomal gene is required to cause a disease.
Answer B: An autosomal recessive disorder is de�ned by the inheritance of two mutated genes. Examples are sickle cell anemia and cystic
�brosis.
Answer C: X-linked disorders refer to genetic conditions associated with mutations in genes on the X-chromosome. Examples include Rett
syndrome and fragile X syndrome.
Answer D: Y-linked disorders are conditions associated with genetic mutations on the Y-chromosome. Examples include congenital adrenal
hyperplasia and Alagille syndrome.

questions.question: Disinhibition, distractibility, and behavior changes are most associated with damage to the ____________ lobe.
questions.explanation:
The frontal lobe is involved in a variety of complex executive functioning tasks, including problem solving and regulating emotions. As a result,
damage to this area can result in disinhibition (impulsivity), distractibility, and various behavior changes.
Answer A: Damage to the parietal lobe may cause right-left confusion (Gerstmann's Syndrome), agraphia (di�culty writing), acalculia (di�culty
with math), aphasia (disorders of language), and/or agnosia (inability to perceive objects normally).
Answer C: Temporal lobe damage may cause disturbances in auditory and visual sensation and/or perception.
Answer D: Damage to the occipital lobe can result in loss of visual capability, inability to identify colors, and hallucinations.

questions.question: Which response is consistent with the James-Lange theory of emotion?

options.B: My heart is racing, therefore I am scared.
options.C: It's noon, so I must be hungry.
options.D: That was a great birthday surprise, so I must be happy.

questions.explanation:
The James-Lange theory of emotion states that an autonomic arousal and skeletal action comes before an emotion. More speci�cally, an
event happens, then you appraise it (the cognitive aspect); this leads to an action (the behavioral aspect), which in turn leads to emotions (the
feeling aspect).
Answer A: This is a phrase coined by the French philosopher René Descartes.
Answer C: This is a feeling based on a time, which does not �t the James-Lange theory of emotion.
Answer D: This answer is a feeling based on an event, which does not follow the James-Lange theory of emotion.

questions.question: A 34-year-old female with a moderate intellectual disability is accompanied by a staff from her group home. The client presents with acute onset confusion, disorientation, combative behaviors, and appears to be responding to internal stimuli. She denies substance use and the group home staff corroborate this. Which of the following is the best �rst course of action?

options.A: Assess for other symptoms of a schizophrenia spectrum disorder and refer to a psychiatrist for psychopharmacological treatment.
options.B: Recommend the group home staff utilize re-orientation techniques and memory cues to help ground the individual and ensure the environment is stable and quiet to prevent further confusion.
options.C: Treat the client’s combative behaviors using principles of Applied Behavior Analysis.
options.D: Refer the client to a primary care physician to rule out a medical condition.

questions.explanation:
The client is presenting with symptoms of delirium, which is due to a physiological cause such as an infection, general medical condition or
substance use/withdrawal. Hallmark symptoms include the acute onset of cognitive changes like disorientation, memory de�cits, perceptual
disturbances, and di�culty shifting attention. While delirium is more common in older adults, it can occur at any age. Once delirium is
suspected, the underlying medical cause must be identi�ed and treated.
Answer A: While assessing for other symptoms of a schizophrenia spectrum disorder and referring to a psychiatrist for medication is
important, the �rst course of action should be to rule out a medical cause, especially due to the acute symptom onset.
Answer B: While treatment strategies for delirium involve reorientation techniques and memory cues, the �rst line of treatment involves
addressing the underlying medical or physiological cause. After the medical concern is addressed, additional strategies for reorienting the
individual and making their treatment environment comfortable are added to complement to the medical treatment and support recovery.
Answer C: This would not be the �rst line of treatment. Although ABA can be used to reduce dangerous or challenging behaviors, while
teaching safer, more functional behaviors for meeting an individual’s needs, the �rst course of action is to rule out a medical condition
impacting the individual’s presentation.

questions.question: Which of the following is true for someone with Broca's aphasia?

options.B: Comprehension is seriously impaired, and it is di�cult to name objects.
options.C: The content of speech used is mostly nouns and verbs with poor pronunciation.
options.D: The content of speech is grammatically correct but often nonsensical.

questions.explanation:
Broca's aphasia is also known as expressive aphasia and is characterized by partial loss of the ability to produce language (spoken, manual, or
written), although comprehension generally remains intact.
Answer A: Wernicke's aphasia best describes unimpaired pronunciation.
Answer B: Impaired comprehension and di�culty naming objects are characteristics of Wernicke's aphasia.
Answer D: Nonsensical grammar aligns with Wernicke's aphasia.

questions.question: A(n) ____________ seizure is typically seen in children and characterized by periods of inattention, lapses in awareness, and staring.
questions.explanation:
During an absence seizure, also referred to as a petit mal seizure, symptoms can include staring off into space, inattention, lapses in
awareness, and repetitive blinking.
Answer A: Tonic phase is the beginning of a grand mal seizure where the muscles contract forcefully.
Answer C: Clonic means agitated. This phase of the seizure begins when the person begins jerking, trembling, and/or convulsing.
Answer D: A simple partial seizure is also referred to as a focal seizure and occurs in only one area of the brain, usually accompanied by an
aura.

questions.question: Agraphia, acalculia, �nger agnosia, and left-right disorientation are symptoms of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Gerstmann Syndrome is a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by agraphia, acalculia, �nger agnosia, and left-right disorientation.
Answer A: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare degenerative brain disease that is characterized by memory loss, behavioral changes, poor
coordination, and visual disturbances.
Answer B: Addison's disease, also known as hypercortisolism, is an endocrine disorder with symptoms including abdominal pain, weakness,
and weight loss.
Answer D: Geschwind syndrome (Gastaut-Geschwind) is a behavioral syndrome associated with temporal lobe epilepsy and is characterized by
circumstantiality (excessive verbal output), hypergraphia (intense desire to write or draw), hyposexuality, emotional volatility, and, in some
cases, hyperreligiosity.

questions.question: Left temporal lobe damage causes which of the following symptoms?

options.A: Word recognition di�culty and impaired verbal memory
options.B: Poor judgment, impulsivity, and inappropriate behavior

questions.explanation:
Left temporal lobe lesions disturb the recognition of words. Additionally, impaired memory for verbal material can result in damage to this area.
Answer B: Damage to the frontal lobe can impair judgment and result in inappropriate behavior and impulsivity.
Answer C: Prosopagnosia occurs as a result of damage to the fusiform gyrus. Agraphia is the loss of ability to communicate through writing.
Answer D: Depression and apathy have been linked to subcortical limbic brain regions and are not always correlated with damage to the brain.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs is most likely to produce anticholinergic effects when administered at therapeutic doses?
questions.explanation:
Chlorpromazine, generic for Thorazine, is a �rst generation antipsychotic. Many typical and atypical antipsychotic medications may cause
anticholinergic effects like dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, dry eyes, confusion, and memory di�culties.
Answer A: Fluoxetine, generic for Prozac, is also an SSRI. Anticholinergic effects are less likely with SSRI use.
Answer B: Fluvoxamine, generic for Luvox, is an SSRI. Most common side effects of SSRI’s include restlessness, insomnia, gastrointestinal
upset, frequent urination, and sexual dysfunction.
Answer D: Carbamazepine, generic for Tegretol, is an anticonvulsant used to treat mania. Side effects may include drowsiness, diarrhea,
nausea/vomiting, and headache. Although carbamazepine toxicity or overdose can be associated with anticholinergic effects, risk is low in
therapeutic doses.

questions.question: Which of the following is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that also possesses analgesic properties?
questions.explanation:
Endorphins or “endogenous morphines” are inhibitory peptide neuromodulators that have analgesic properties and support the regulation of
stress and pain.
Answer A: Glutamate is an excitatory neurotransmitter that is thought to play a role in the formation of long-term memories. Abnormal
glutamate transmission is also associated with schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, depression, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Answer B: Dopamine is linked to thought, movement, and emotion, and plays a large role in the brain’s reward system. The dopamine
hypothesis explains how an excess of dopamine can result in the psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia.
Answer D: GABA is an amino acid and major inhibitory neurotransmitter that has a calming effect, and insu�cient levels of GABA are often
associated with anxiety.

questions.question: Early memory loss associated with Alzheimer's disease is believed to be caused by deterioration of neurons in the hippocampus that secrete:
questions.explanation:
Acetylcholine (ACh) mediates motor functions as well as learning processes, and lower levels of ACh in the hippocampus have been linked to
decreased alertness in Alzheimer's patients.
Answer A: Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid (GABA) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter. It decreases activity in the nervous system and plays a role in
stress, anxiety, and fear.
Answer B: Serotonin has been linked to a variety of functions, including emotions and motor skills. Abnormalities in serotonin levels have been
linked to sleep, appetite, and mood in Alzheimer's patients.
Answer C: Dopamine is responsible for transmitting signals between neurons in the brain. Dopamine pathways are involved in motor control
and the release of various hormones.

questions.question: Damage to the hippocampus is most likely to interfere with the ability to:

options.C: convert short-term memory to long-term memory.

questions.explanation:
The hippocampus is involved in converting immediate (short-term) memories into long-term memories.
Answer A: The hippocampus does not play a role in retrieving long-term memories.
Answer B: The hippocampus does not contribute to the manipulation of information.
Answer D: The amygdala plays a role in storing memories.

questions.question: Eating foods containing tyramine (e.g., cheese, raisins) while taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) is contraindicated because which of the following can occur?
questions.explanation:
Taking an MAOI in combination with foods containing tyramine can cause an increase in blood pressure.
Answer A: A rebound effect occurs when the emergence or re-emergence of symptoms that were either absent or controlled while taking a
medication appear after the medication has been discontinued.
Answer B: Agranulocytosis is an acute symptom involving a severe and dangerous leukopenia (lowered white blood cell count) that leads to a
weakened immune system.
Answer C: Tardive dyskinesia is a disorder that results in involuntary, repetitive body movements.

questions.question: Which of the following is a second-generation antipsychotic?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone is a second-generation antipsychotic (atypical antipsychotic) that alleviates symptoms of schizophrenia without producing
movement problems.
Answer A: Paroxetine (Paxil) is a common selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that is similar to a tricyclic but has milder side effects.
Answer B: Phenelzine is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MOAI).
Answer C: Fluoxetine (Prozac) is an SSRI.

questions.question: The ability to recognize the color of an object despite changes in the lighting is de�ned as which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Color constancy is the ability to recognize something as being the same color despite changes in lighting. Area 4 is important for color
constancy.
Answer A: Motion perception is the process of inferring the speed and direction of elements in a scene based on visual, vestibular, and
proprioceptive inputs.
Answer C: A saccade is a quick, simultaneous movement of both eyes between two or more phases of �xation in the same direction.
Answer D: Visual agnosia is an inability to recognize objects despite otherwise satisfactory vision.

questions.question: Individuals who have sustained a traumatic brain injury are most likely to _____

options.A: experience retrograde amnesia only and as they recover their memories, they’re more likely to recall recent events �rst and then slowly begin to recall more remote events.
options.B: experience retrograde and anterograde amnesia and as they recover their memories, they’re more likely to recall remote events �rst and then slowly recall more recent events.
options.C: experience anterograde amnesia only and as they recover their memories, they’re more likely to recall remote events �rst and then slowly recall more recent events.
options.D: experience anterograde and retrograde amnesia and as they recover their memories, they’re more likely to recall recent events �rst and then slowly begin to recall more remote events.

questions.explanation:
When an individual sustains a head trauma, they tend to suffer from both retrograde amnesia or the inability to recall events that occurred prior
to the trauma and anterograde amnesia, di�culty forming new memories. As an individual recovers, they will remember remote memories �rst,
followed by more recent memories leading up to the trauma, and �nally, the ability to form new memories.
Answer A: Individuals tend to experience both retrograde and anterograde amnesia after a traumatic brain injury and are more likely to
remember remote memories �rst, followed by slowly recalling more recent memories.
Answer C: This answer is partially correct in that remote memories are more easily recalled than recent memories; however, an individual
sustaining a head trauma is more likely to experience memory loss for events prior to the trauma (retrograde amnesia) and the inability to form
new memories (anterograde amnesia).
Answer D: Individuals experiencing a head trauma are more likely to experience both retrograde and anterograde amnesia, and when they do
recall their memories, they typically recall more remote memories �rst, followed by recent memories.

questions.question: What class of chemicals prevents apoptosis?
questions.explanation:
Neurotrophins are a class of proteins that induce the survival, development, and function of neurons. Nerve growth factor (NGF) is a type of
neurotrophin that cancels the program for apoptosis.
Answer B: Leukocytes are part of the body's immune system, which helps �ght infection and other diseases.
Answer C: Prolactin is the hormone that tells the body to make breast milk.
Answer D: Axons are the part of the neuron that transmits electrical impulses.

questions.question: Which part of the autonomic nervous system facilitates vegetative, nonemergency responses.?
questions.explanation:
The parasympathetic system is one of the two branches related to the autonomic nervous system. This speci�c part is called the rest and
digest system.
Answer A: The sympathetic nervous system directs the body's rapid involuntary response to dangerous or stressful situations.
Answer B: The central nervous system controls most functions of the body and the mind.
Answer C: The main function of the peripheral nervous system is to connect the central nervous system to the limbs and organs.

questions.question: Benzodiazepines with a short half-life (e.g., triazolam, midazolam) can cause which type of amnesia for a short period after the drug has worn off?
questions.explanation:
Anterograde amnesia is the loss of memory for a short period after a drug has worn off.
Answer A: Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memory access to events that occurred or information that was learned in the past.
Answer C: Transient global amnesia is a sudden, temporary episode of memory loss that cannot be attributed to a more common neurological
condition.
Answer D: Infantile amnesia (childhood amnesia) is the inability of adults to retrieve episodic memories (memories of situations or events)
before the age of two to four years old.

questions.question: A split-brain patient (patient with callosal syndrome) would likely be able to:

options.A: verbalize the word "spoon" after it has been projected to his left visual �eld.
options.B: repeat a series of letters that have been whispered in his left ear.
options.C: verbally identify an odor that has been presented to his right nostril.
options.D: identify a spoon with his left hand after an image of a spoon has been projected to his left visual �eld.

questions.explanation:
An image presented to the left visual �eld would be processed in the right hemisphere, which controls the left hand. Therefore, a split-brain
patient would be able to perform this task.
Answer A: Information projected to the left visual �eld would be transmitted directly to the right hemisphere. A split-brain patient would not be
able to verbalize what he just saw.
Answer B: Information that entered the left ear would be delivered to the right hemisphere. Consequently, the split-brain patient would not be
able to repeat the information.
Answer C: Olfactory signals do not cross the opposite side of the brain; therefore, stimulation that has entered the right nostril would be
delivered to the right hemisphere.

questions.question: A psychologist is attempting to assess the general intelligence of a six-year-old child with a severe hearing impairment. Which of the following tests would be most effective?
questions.explanation:
The Hiskey-Nebraska Test of Learning Aptitude is a measure of learning ability for children and adolescents ages 3:0 to 17:6 who have hearing
or language impairments. It can be administered verbally or in pantomime.
Answer A: The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery is a measure used to detect the presence of brain damage and determine its
severity and possible location in individuals ages 15 and older.
Answer B: The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC-II) is a measure of cognitive ability for children ages 3:0 to 18:11. While
administration of the KABC-II does minimize the need for verbal instructions and responses, this is with intent to be culturally fair.
Answer C: The Haptic Intelligence Scale for the Adult Blind is a measure for adolescents and adults (16:0 and older) who are blind or partially
sighted.

questions.question: A psychologist administers the Wisconsin Card Sort Category Test and the Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery when evaluating a patient for brain damage. The psychologist likely believes that the patient has:
questions.explanation:
The frontal lobe is involved in a number of functions including initiative, planning, and sequential task completion. Damage to the frontal lobe
signi�cantly impacts performance on the Wisconsin Card Sort and Halstead-Reitan Category Test, as strong performances on these tests are
contingent on intact frontal lobe functioning.
Answer A: The assessments listed are used to assess frontal lobe functioning and lateral functioning, not diffuse brain functioning.
Answer C: The assessments listed are used to assess frontal lobe functioning and lateral functioning, not temporal lobe functioning.
Answer D: The assessments listed are used to assess frontal lobe functioning and lateral functioning, not functioning associated with the basal
ganglia.

questions.question: A person with a realistic orientation will likely be satis�ed with job tasks that ____________, according to Holland's theory about the importance of matching a person's personality with their work environment.

options.B: require mechanical, physical, and technical skills
options.C: are unambiguous and require the organization of data
options.D: require scholarly analytical skills, such as scienti�c or mathematical activities

questions.explanation:
Holland's six personality types are realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, and conventional ("RIASEC"). Individuals with a realistic
personality type likely will be satis�ed with job tasks that require mechanical, physical, and technical skills.
Answer A: Individuals with an artistic personality type likely will be satis�ed with job tasks that require creativity.
Answer C: Individuals with a conventional personality type likely will be satis�ed with job tasks that are unambiguous and require the
organization of data.
Answer D: Individuals with an investigative personality type likely will be satis�ed with job tasks that require scholarly analytical skills, such as
scienti�c or mathematical activities.

questions.question: The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT) was designed as a measure of receptive vocabulary for:

options.A: adolescents and adults with a visual impairment.
options.B: children and adolescents with a hearing or language impairment.
options.C: children, adolescents, and adults with autism.
options.D: children, adolescents, and adults with a motor or speech impairment.

questions.explanation:
The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT) is a measure of receptive vocabulary developed to assess children, adolescents, and adults with
a motor or a speech impairment. During the assessment, examiners ask examinees to point to (or otherwise indicate) the picture that best
corresponds to the word verbally provided by the examiner.
Answer A: The Haptic Intelligence Scale is a measure designed for adolescents and adults with visual impairments.
Answer B: The Hiskey-Nebraska Test is a measure of intelligence for children and adolescents with a hearing or a language impairment.
Answer C: The PPVT is a measure of receptive vocabulary developed to assess children, adolescents, and adults with a motor or a speech
impairment, not individuals with autism speci�cally.

questions.question: The developer of a new occupational interest test conducts a study to determine which test items accurately distinguish between people who are employed in different occupations. The test developer is likely using which of the following methods of scale construction?
questions.explanation:
The test developer is trying to determine which items distinguish between speci�c criterion groups (i.e., people employed in different
occupations). Empirical criterion keying involves choosing items for different scales on the basis of how well the items distinguish between
different criterion groups. This method was used in the development of the Kuder Occupational Interest Survey as well as the Occupational
scales of the Strong Interest Inventory.
Answer B: Homogeneous keying is used when items are selected on the basis of the degree to which they measure the same domain.
Answer C: Factor analysis entails administering a large pool of items to examinees, factor analyzing the intercorrelations of items to identify
underlying factors (traits), labeling the identi�ed factors, and including items in the test so that each factor is adequately assessed.
Answer D: Multiple regression analysis is a multivariate technique that is useful when performance on two or more predictors will be used to
estimate an individual's score on a criterion. It is not a method of scale construction.

questions.question: On the Rorschach Inkblot Test, confabulation is most suggestive of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Confabulation on the Rorschach refers to overgeneralizing a part of the inkblot to the whole. Confabulation is associated with brain damage,
emotional disturbance, or intellectual disability.
Answers A, B, and C: Confabulation is associated with brain damage, emotional disturbance, or intellectual disability.

questions.question: The IQ concordance rate for biological (non-twin) siblings who are reared together is:
questions.explanation:
The contribution of heredity to IQ is con�rmed by studies showing that the greater the genetic similarity, the higher the concordance rate.
Bouchard and Gue report an IQ concordance rate of 0.45 for biological (non-twin) siblings reared together.
Answer A: The IQ concordance rate for identical twins reared together is 0.85.
Answer B: The IQ concordance rate for identical twins reared apart is 0.67.
Answer D: The IQ concordance rate for biological parent and child living apart is 0.22.

questions.question: In the case of Larry P. v. Riles, the court ruled that IQ tests:

options.C: are valid predictors of job performance for members of minority groups when used in conjunction with other measures.
options.D: are valid measures of intelligence for members of minority groups when administered by an examiner of the same race/ethnicity.

questions.explanation:
In the Larry P. v. Riles case, a suit was brought against the California State Department of Education and the San Francisco School Board on the
grounds that the use of standardized IQ tests as a placement technique resulted in an over-representation of African American children in
special education classes. Following expert testimony, the judge determined that IQ tests are racially and culturally biased, as well as have a
discriminatory impact on Black children. The judge enjoined San Francisco public schools from using IQ tests to place Black children in special
education classes, indicating they should not be used as placement tools for children of color.
Answer A: The court found that standardized IQ assessments are racially and culturally biased.
Answer C: The court case was not focused on job performance.
Answer D: The court did not �nd that the bias in standardized intellectual assessments is mitigated by the examiner's race/ethnicity.

questions.question: The Bender-Gestalt II is a measure of:
questions.explanation:
The Bender-Gestalt II is a brief assessment of visual-motor integration. During administration, the examinee copies geometric �gures and then
draws them from memory. It is used to assess visual-motor integration and assist in the assessment of neurological impairment.
Answer A: While �ne motor skills in�uence performance on the Bender-Gestalt II, the test is a measure of visual-motor integration.
Answer C: The Bender-Gestalt II does not assess cognitive �exibility.
Answer D: The Bender-Gestalt II does not measure suicidality.

questions.question: A psychologist administers the MMPI-2 to a 36-year old man who exhibits a number of symptoms suggestive of neurosis. The man receives a very low K scale score. On the basis of this score, the psychologist can tentatively conclude that the man:

options.A: tried to present himself in a favorable light.
options.D: may have an organic brain disorder.

questions.explanation:
The K (Correction) scale is one of the MMPI's validity scales. A very low score on the K scale indicates excessive frankness, self-criticism, or an
attempt to "fake bad."
Answer A: An elevated K score might indicate an attempt to "fake good."
Answer C: The MMPI-2's validity scales were not designed to provide information about personality disorders.
Answer D: The MMPI-2's validity scales were not designed to detect organic brain disorders.

questions.question: Anna is in the process of buying a new car and is having trouble deciding between two cars that are similar in terms of both positive and negative characteristics. In other words, Anna is facing a(n) ____________ con�ict.
questions.explanation:
As its name implies, a double approach–avoidance con�ict occurs when a person has to choose between two objects or events that have both
positive and negative qualities.
Answer A: An approach-approach con�ict occurs when a person has to choose between two equally positive events or objects. In this case, the
two cars have both positive and negative characteristics, so this is not the best answer.
Answer B: An avoidance-avoidance con�ict occurs when a person has to choose between two equally undesirable events or objects. Again,
because the cars have both positive and negative qualities, this is not the best answer.
Answer C: A single approach–avoidance con�ict occurs when a single object or event has both positive and negative qualities. Additional
information about these con�icts is presented in the Social Psychology chapter of the written study materials.

questions.question: Mary thinks her teacher is a real jerk for always assigning weekend homework. Mary's belief about her teacher is best explained by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to attribute another person's behavior to dispositional factors (e.g., traits) and, therefore, to
expect a great deal of consistency in behavior.
Answer A: The overjusti�cation hypothesis predicts that internal motivation to perform a speci�c action is weakened when one is given
external reinforcement for performing the action.
Answer B: The self-serving bias applies to the attributions one makes about one's own behavior and is not relevant to the situation described in
this question.
Answer D: Self-veri�cation theory predicts that people prefer receiving information about themselves from others that is consistent with their
self-evaluations.

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates deindividuation?

options.A: A usually quiet, reserved person acts uncharacteristically violent in a crowd because he is able to do so anonymously.
options.B: A victim of a crime is more likely to receive assistance when the crime occurs in a rural area rather than in a city.
options.C: In a group decision-making situation, there is a tendency for critical thinking to be suspended when group cohesiveness is very strong.
options.D: A group member reduces her effort when she thinks other members are not exerting maximum effort.

questions.explanation:
Deindividuation occurs in conditions that foster a loss of personal identity.
Answer B: This describes "bystander apathy."
Answer C: This describes "groupthink."
Answer D: This is referred to as the "sucker effect."

questions.question: With regard to attitude change, inoculation is useful for:

options.A: increasing a person's resistance to persuasion.
options.B: reducing a communicator's anxiety prior to delivering a message to a hostile audience.
options.C: distracting a person from a communicator's message.
options.D: ensuring that attitude change represents internalization rather than mere compliance.

questions.explanation:
The concept of inoculation (McGuire, 1969) was derived from the medical model and is based on the assumption that a person will be better
able to resist a persuasive communication when they have been "inoculated" against it. Inoculation involves providing weak arguments against
a position and counterarguments refuting those arguments. Inoculation has been shown to be an effective method for increasing an
individual's resistance to persuasion.
Answer B: This is not the goal of inoculation.
Answer C: Distraction is associated with increased persuasiveness when a listener is initially opposed to a message and decreased
persuasiveness when a listener is initially in favor of a message. Inoculation does not involve distraction.
Answer D: This is not a goal of inoculation.

questions.question: Superordinate goals have been found useful for:

options.C: reducing intergroup con�ict in order for opposing sides to reach common goals.

questions.explanation:
Superordinate goals are those that allow opposing sides to work together toward a common goal. In their famous Robber's Cave study (1961),
Sherif and his colleagues found that the introduction of superordinate goals was the most effective way of reducing intergroup hostility,
allowing for joint efforts toward the common goal.
Answer A: Clarifying roles is not the objective of superordinate goals.
Answer B: Maximizing satisfaction and motivation are not the objectives of superordinate goals.
Answer D: Superordinate goals can be achieved only through intergroup cooperation, not merely individual efforts. These topics are all
described in the Social Psychology chapter of the written study materials.

questions.question: According to Bem's self-perception theory (1972):

options.A: people experience discomfort (dissonance) when their behaviors are not consistent with their attitudes, beliefs, or values.
options.B: people enhance their own sense of self-worth by associating or identifying with others who are successful.
options.C: people tend to attribute their successes to dispositional factors and failures to situational factors.
options.D: people infer their own attitudes and emotions by observing their behaviors and the circumstances in which those behaviors occur.

questions.explanation:
Bem's self-perception theory predicts that when people aren't certain about their own attitudes and feelings, they make inferences about them
based on their behavior, in the same way that they determine the states of other people.
Answer A: This relates to cognitive dissonance theory, not self-perception theory.
Answer B: This is not a prediction made by self-perception theory.
Answer C: This answer describes the self-serving bias.

questions.question: The tendency to seek out and interpret information in ways that verify our existing beliefs is referred to as the:
questions.explanation:
The con�rmation bias is a cognitive bias which, as its name implies, involves focusing on and seeking out information that con�rms our
preconceptions.
Answer A: The hindsight bias refers to the tendency to believe that, after an outcome occurs, you could have predicted the outcome
beforehand.
Answer B: The primacy effect refers to the tendency to remember material that occurred �rst better than material that occurred last.
Answer C: The focusing effect is the tendency to place too much importance (focus) on one aspect of an event or situation when predicting a
future outcome.

questions.question: The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) predicts that:

options.A: attitudes are the result of behaviors.
options.B: attitudes are the result of subjective norms, behavioral intentions, and behaviors.
options.C: behaviors are the result of attitudes.
options.D: behaviors are the result of attitudes, subjective norms, and behavioral intentions.

questions.explanation:
Ajzen's theory of planned behavior (1991) attributes behaviors to three factors: attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and the
intention to perform the behavior (behavioral intention).
Answers A, B, and C: Behaviors are the result of attitudes, subjective norms, and intentions.

questions.question: The three components of attitudes are:
questions.explanation:
The three components of attitudes, as suggested by the ABC Model of Attitudes, are affect, behavior, and cognition.
Answers B, C, and D: Attitudes comprise affect, behavior, and cognition.

questions.question: Individuals who frequently view violent TV shows:

options.A: tend to fear their environment more than those who view less TV violence.
options.B: fear their environment somewhat less than people who report being less frequent viewers.
options.C: fear their environment much less than people who report being less frequent viewers.
options.D: are about equal in terms of fear of their environment to people who report being less frequent viewers.

questions.explanation:
The results of the studies are not entirely consistent, but, overall, they indicate that frequent viewing of media violence is associated with an
increased fear of the environment.
Answers B, C, and D: Frequent viewing of media violence is associated with an increased, not decreased or equal, fear of the environment.

questions.question: A researcher would use the randomized block ANOVA to analyze collected data in order to:

options.A: analyze the main and interaction effects of an extraneous variable.
options.C: evaluate the effects of an independent variable on multiple dependent variables.
options.D: evaluate the effects of one or more independent variables on a nominal dependent variable.

questions.explanation:
The randomized block ANOVA is the appropriate inferential statistical test when a researcher uses blocking to control for an extraneous
variable. When using the randomized block ANOVA, the extraneous ("blocking") variable is treated like an independent variable so that the
respective researcher can evaluate its main and interaction effects on the dependent variable.
Answer B: A randomized block ANOVA would not be useful for controlling for measurement error. To control for measurement error, a
researcher would place emphasis on study design strategies for increasing reliability and validity.
Answer C: A MANOVA would be useful for this purpose.
Answer D: The chi-square test would be useful for this purpose.

questions.question: If a researcher has found heteroscedasticity in a scattergram, they have found that:

options.A: the relationship between the predictor and criterion cannot be described by a straight line.
options.B: there is a restriction of range of scores on the predictor and/or the criterion.
options.C: the variability (range) of scores on the criterion varies for different scores on the predictor.
options.D: there is a statistically signi�cant correlation between the predictor and criterion.

questions.explanation:
Heteroscedasticity means unequal variability. Heteroscedasticity occurs when the variability of scores on the criterion differs for different
scores on the predictor (e.g., when there is a narrow range of criterion scores for low and high predictor scores but a wide range of criterion
scores for moderate predictor scores). A �gure illustrating heteroscedasticity and homoscedasticity is included in the Statistics and Research
Design chapter of the written study materials.
Answer A: This is not a conclusion that can be drawn from knowing that there is heteroscedasticity in a scattergram. This is more re�ective of
a non-linear relationship between variables.
Answer B: This is not a conclusion that can be drawn from knowing that there is heteroscedasticity in a scattergram. A restricted range may
show a linear relationship, but it will not show an unequal scatter (scattering) or the characteristic "funnel" shape.
Answer D: This is not a conclusion that can be drawn from knowing that there is heteroscedasticity in a scattergram. A statistically signi�cant
correlation between the predictor and criterion would be well �tted to the regression line and not vary across vectors as plots of
heteroscedasticity do.

questions.question: Researchers usually prefer parametric statistical tests over non-parametric tests because they are more "powerful." This means that the use of a parametric test to analyze collected data in a research study helps ensure that:

options.A: a false null hypothesis will be retained.
options.B: a true null hypothesis will be retained.
options.C: a false null hypothesis will be rejected.
options.D: the null hypothesis will be rejected.

questions.explanation:
Statistical power is the ability to detect a false null hypothesis. Rejecting a false null hypothesis is an accurate description of power. Note: If
you're having trouble remembering what power is or what the difference between a Type I and a Type II error is, the Decision Outcomes table in
the Statistics and Research Design chapter may be helpful.
Answer A: Retaining a false null hypothesis is a Type II error.
Answer B: This is not a description of power. Power refers to the ability to reject a null hypothesis when it is false, or the probability of avoiding
a Type II error.
Answer D: Power is the ability to reject a false null hypothesis, not just to the ability to reject any null hypothesis.

questions.question: Which of the following techniques would be most useful for obtaining information on the cognitive processes used by students while they solve complex problems?
questions.explanation:
Protocol analysis (also known as the "think aloud" technique) is used to identify the mental processes that occur during the solution of
problems or the performance of tasks. Of the techniques listed, protocol analysis is the only one researchers use to study cognitive processes.
Answer A: Event sampling is a behavioral observation and data collection technique that is useful when the behavior of interest occurs
infrequently.
Answer B: Situation sampling is a behavioral observation and data collection technique that involves observing a behavior in a variety of
situations.
Answer C: A functional analysis is used to identify the functions of a behavior (i.e., the antecedents and consequences that maintain the
behavior).

questions.question: Of 100 students surveyed on a college campus, 48 voted Republican and 52 voted Democrat in the last election. On another college campus, 63 of the 100 students surveyed voted Republican and 37 voted Democrat. Which of the following statistical tests is the appropriate technique for determining if there is a statistically signi�cant difference in voting preferences at the two colleges?
questions.explanation:
The chi-square test is used when data are reported as the frequency of observations, which is the case in this study (i.e., the analysis will
involve comparing the frequencies (numbers) of Republican and Democrat voters at the two schools.
Answer A: The two-way ANOVA is used when a study involves two independent variables and data on the dependent variable represent an
interval or ratio scale.
Answer B: The t-test is used to compare two means.
Answer D: The Mann-Whitney U test is used when the analysis involves comparing rank-ordered data obtained from two independent samples.

questions.question: When the relationship between the predictor (the X variable) and the criterion (the Y variable) is curvilinear and both variables are measured on an interval or ratio scale, the appropriate correlation coe�cient is:
questions.explanation:
Eta is used to measure the relationship between two continuous (interval or ratio) variables when their relationship is nonlinear. The choice of a
correlation coe�cient is based on several factors including the scale of measurement of the variables and the shape of the relationship
between them (linear vs. non-linear).
Answer A: The phi coe�cient is appropriate when both variables are true (natural) dichotomies.
Answer B: Kendall's tau is appropriate when both variables are measured on an ordinal scale.
Answer C: Rho (also known as the Spearman rank-order correlation coe�cient) is used when both variables are measured as ranks.

questions.question: The magnitude of the standard error of the mean increases as:

options.A: the sample size increases and the population variance decreases.
options.B: the sample size and population variance both increase.
options.C: the sample size and population variance both decrease.
options.D: the sample size decreases and the population variance increases.

questions.explanation:
Knowing the formula for the standard error of the mean will help you identify the correct answer to this question. The standard error of the
mean is equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. As the population standard deviation
increases and/or the sample size decreases, the standard error increases in magnitude. Refer to the Statistics and Research Design chapter of
the written study materials for a more detailed description of the standard error of the mean.
Answer A: This is the opposite of what would occur. As the magnitude of the standard error of the mean increases, the sample size decreases
and the population variance increases.
Answer B: As the magnitude of the standard error of the mean increases, the sample size would decrease, not increase.
Answer C: Half of this statement is correct; the sample size would decrease when the magnitude of the standard error of the mean increases.
However, as the magnitude of the standard error of the mean increases, the population variance would also increase, not decrease.

questions.question: Autocorrelation is most likely to be a problem when using which of the following research designs?
questions.explanation:
Autocorrelation refers to the correlation between measurements of the dependent variable when it is repeatedly administered to the same
participants. Autocorrelation is a problem in repeated measures designs because it can arti�cially in�ate the value of the inferential statistic,
which will increase the probability of making a Type I error. Of the research designs listed in the answers, repeated measurement of the
dependent variable is only characteristic of the time series design, which is a type of repeated measures (within subjects) design.
Answer B: Factorial designs include two or more independent variables and do not necessarily involve repeated measurements of the
dependent variable.
Answer C: Autocorrelation refers to the correlation between measurements of the dependent variable when it is repeatedly administered to the
same participants. A between groups design is used to compare outcomes (measurements of the dependent variable) between different
groups of participants and does not directly relate to in�ated values and the increased probability of making a Type I error.
Answer D: The Solomon four-group design is used evaluate the impact of pretesting and does not relate to in�ated statistical values and the
increased probability of making a Type I error.

questions.question: When using multiple regression, multicollinearity occurs when:

options.A: the predictors are highly correlated with one another.
options.B: the criterion measures are highly correlated with one another.
options.C: there is a low correlation between the predictors and the criterion.
options.D: there is a high (signi�cant) correlation between the predictors and the criterion.

questions.explanation:
The term "multicollinearity" is used to describe high correlations between predictors (X variables). Additional information on multiple
regression and multicollinearity is in the Statistics and Research Design chapter of the written study materials.
Answer B: Multicollinearity occurs when the predictors (i.e., independent variables) are highly correlated with one another, not the criterion (i.e.,
dependent) variables.
Answer C: Multicollinearity occurs when the predictors (i.e., independent variables) are highly correlated with one another, not when there is a
low correlation between the predictors and criterion.
Answer D: Multicollinearity occurs when the predictors are highly correlated with one another, not when the predictors and criterion are highly
correlated.

questions.question: You would use the Solomon four-group design in order to:

options.D: evaluate the effects of history and maturation.

questions.explanation:
The purpose of the Solomon four-group design is to evaluate the impact of pretesting on a study's internal and external validity. The Solomon
four-group design combines the pretest-posttest control group design with the posttest-only control group design.
Answer A: Effects that carry over from one experimental condition to another are not related to the Solomon four-group design; you would use
a Latin Square design or counterbalancing to account for carryover effects.
Answer B: You would not use the Solomon four-group design to correct for bias created by the experimenter's expectations or participants'
perceptions of the purpose of the study.
Answer D: The purpose of the Solomon four-group design is to evaluate the impact of pretesting on a study's internal and external validity.
While history and maturation are considered threats to the internal consistency aspect of validity, you would typically address history and
maturation by reducing the amount of time between the pretest and posttest.

questions.question: The hallmark of true experimental research, in contrast to quasi-experimental research, is that a researcher would:

options.A: operationally de�ne the independent and dependent variables.
options.B: use parametric tests to analyze the obtained data.
options.C: randomly select participants from the population.
options.D: randomly assign participants to treatment groups.

questions.explanation:
The key feature distinguishing true experimental research from quasi-experimental research is the ability to randomly assign participants to
groups so that a researcher can make causal inferences about the relationships between variables. This is the hallmark of true experimental
research.
Answer A: An operational de�nition is a precise description of a variable in a way that facilitates its measurement. Variables are operationally
de�ned when using either a true or quasi-experimental research strategy.
Answer B: The choice of a parametric or nonparametric statistical test is based on the characteristics of the data, not the research strategy
used.
Answer C: Random selection is not a requirement for either true or quasi-experimental research. For the EPPP, you will need to know the
difference between random assignment to groups and random sampling. Refer to the Statistics and Research Design chapter of the written
study materials for clari�cation.

questions.question: A distribution of 250 scores is positively skewed and has a range of 1 to 50. In this distribution, which of the following is an accurate description of the measures of central tendency in relationship to one another?

options.A: The median is the highest score and the mean is the lowest score.
options.B: The mode is the highest score and the mean is the lowest score.
options.C: The mean is the highest score and the mode is the lowest score.
options.D: The mean is the highest score and the median is the lowest score.

questions.explanation:
In a positively skewed distribution, the "tail" is extended on the high side of the distribution (i.e., most of the scores are "piled up" in the low end
of the distribution, while a few scores are in the high end). In this distribution, the mean is the highest value, the mode is the lowest value, and
the median is between the mean and the mode. A �gure illustrating the relationship between the mean, median, and mode in skewed
distributions is included in the Statistics and Research Design chapter of the written study materials.
Answer A: The median is de�ned as the midpoint of a frequency distribution, so it cannot be the highest score. If the mean were the lowest
score, this would result in a negatively skewed distribution.
Answer B: The mode is the most frequently occurring score. When the mode is the highest score and the mean is the lowest score, this would
be a negatively skewed distribution.
Answer D: The mean would be the highest score in a positively skewed distribution, but the median would be the middle score as it is de�ned
as the midpoint of a frequency distribution. By de�nition, the median cannot be the lowest or highest score.

questions.question: When using stepwise multiple regression to explain the greatest amount of variation in Y using the fewest possible X variables, you:

options.A: use the Spearman-Brown formula to adjust the size of the multiple correlation coe�cient as each X variable is added or subtracted.
options.B: use R-squared (coe�cient of multiple determination) to determine if predictability is substantially affected by adding or subtracting another X variable.
options.C: use r (zero order correlation coe�cient) to determine which X variable has the highest correlation with the X variables already introduced into the equation.
options.D: use the eigenvalues to determine which predictor explains the greatest proportion of the remaining variability in Y.

questions.explanation:
The coe�cient of multiple determination (which is the squared value of R) is used to determine if adding or subtracting a predictor has a
signi�cant effect on the proportion of variability in Y that has been explained by the predictors included in the multiple regression equation.
Recalling that multiple regression is used for the purpose of prediction will help you pick the correct response.
Answer A: The Spearman-Brown formula is used to estimate the effects of increasing or decreasing the length of a test on its reliability
coe�cient and is not used in this situation.
Answer C: It is important to check the correlations between the predictors in order to avoid the problem of multicollinearity, but this is not the
best response.
Answer D: You should associate the term "eigenvalues" with principal components analysis, not multiple regression.

questions.question: A group of 250 high school seniors took an achievement test. The test's mean was 50, its standard deviation was 5, and the test scores were normally distributed. If you wanted to use test scores to select the top 16% of the students, you would set the cutoff score at:
questions.explanation:
50% of examinees obtain scores at or below the mean, and an additional 34% obtain scores that fall between the mean and one standard
deviation above the mean in a normal distribution; 50% plus 34% equals 84%. Consequently, the score that is one standard deviation above the
mean divides the distribution into two sections: 84% of the people in the distribution obtain scores at or below one standard deviation above
the mean and the remaining 16% obtain higher scores. The test described in this question has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 5, so
the score that is one standard deviation above the mean is 55.
Answer B: A score of 60 would be two standard deviations above the mean and would represent approximately the top 2.5% of students.
Answer C: A score of 65 would be three standard deviations above the mean and would represent the top .01 % of students.
Answer D: A score of 70 would be four standard deviations above the mean.

questions.question: When a test's reliability has been estimated by splitting the test in half and correlating scores on the two halves, you would use which of the following to correct the resulting reliability coe�cient?
questions.explanation:
Split-half reliability tends to underestimate a measure's reliability. Consequently, a correction formula is often used to estimate the measure's
reliability coe�cient if the measure was based on the full length of the test. The Spearman-Brown formula (also known as the Spearman-Brown
prophecy formula) is commonly used to correct the split-half reliability coe�cient but can also be used to estimate the reliability coe�cient of
a test after it has been lengthened or shortened.
Answer A: The correction for attenuation formula is used to estimate the predictor's validity coe�cient if the predictor and/or criterion were
perfectly reliable.
Answer B: The standard error of measurement is used to calculate the range within which an examinee's true score is likely to fall given their
obtained score.
Answer C: Kuder-Richardson 20 (KR-20) is a type of internal consistency reliability measure that is used when test items are scored
dichotomously.

questions.question: Which of the following would be useful for determining the extent to which an examinee's actual criterion score is likely to deviate from their predicted criterion score?
questions.explanation:
The relationship between a predictor and a criterion is never "perfect." A predicted criterion score may, or may not, be the actual criterion score.
The standard error of estimate is used to construct the range within which an examinee's true criterion score is likely to fall given their
predicted criterion score. This range is referred to as a con�dence interval.
Answer B: The standard error of measurement is used to construct a con�dence interval around an examinee's obtained (not predicted) score.
Answer C: The standard error of the difference is used to determine whether a difference score is signi�cant. A difference score compares two
test scores and contains measurement error from both test scores.
Answer D: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of means and is not used to construct a
con�dence interval around a predicted score.

questions.question: An educational psychologist designs a screening test to identify underachieving �rst- and second-grade children who have a learning disability. The psychologist should be most concerned that her test has adequate ____________ validity.
questions.explanation:
Concurrent validity is a type of criterion-related validity and is of concern when the purpose of the test is to estimate an individual's current
status on some external criterion. Screening tests are typically used to estimate the results of a more thorough evaluation (the criterion), which,
in this case, would be a more thorough diagnostic procedure.
Answer A: Content validity is of most concern when test items are expected to be a representative sample of a particular content domain.
Answer B: Construct validity is of concern for tests designed to measure a hypothetical trait or construct such as motivation or self-esteem.
Answer D: The screening test is being used to estimate current status and not to predict future status. As such, concurrent validity is of greater
concern than predictive validity.

questions.question: An assumption underlying ____________ is that observed covariation among a set of variables is due to one or more underlying common dimensions.
questions.explanation:
The primary function of factor analysis is to identify the factors that underlie the intercorrelations among a set of variables. Covariation is
another word for correlation, so this question is asking what technique is used to determine what accounts for the intercorrelations among a
set of variables.
Answer B: Path analysis is used to test causal models for the relationships among a set of variables.
Answer C: Trend analysis is a type of analysis of variance that is used to assess linear and nonlinear trends when the independent variable is
quantitative.
Answer D: Multiple regression is used to predict a score on a criterion based on scores of two or more predictors.

questions.question: An item discrimination index (D) of _____ indicates that all examinees in the high-scoring group and none in the low- scoring group answered the item correctly.
questions.explanation:
An item discrimination index of +1.0 indicates that all of the high-scoring and none of the low-scoring examinees answered the item correctly.
The item discrimination index ranges from -1.0 to +1.0 and is calculated by subtracting the percent of low-scoring examinees who answered
the item correctly (examinees who obtained low total scores on the test) from the percent of high-scoring examinees who answered the item
correctly (examinees who obtained high total scores on the test).
Answer B: An item discrimination index of -1.0 indicates that all of the low-scoring and none of the high-scoring examinees answered the item
correctly.
Answer C: An item discrimination index of .50 indicates that the 50% fewer of the examinees in the low-scoring group (versus the high-scoring
group) answered the item correctly.
Answer D: An item discrimination index of 0 indicates that the same percent of examinees in the low- and high-scoring groups answered the
item correctly.

questions.question: When a predictor's reliability coe�cient is .81, its criterion-related validity coe�cient can be:
questions.explanation:
A test's reliability limits its validity; that is, an unreliable test cannot be valid. A predictor's validity coe�cient can be no greater than the square
root of its reliability coe�cient. In this situation, the predictor's reliability coe�cient is .81, so its validity coe�cient can be no greater than the
square root of .81, which is .90.
Answer A: The formula for the relationship between a predictor's reliability and validity requires the square root of the predictor's reliability
coe�cient. An answer of .81 does not re�ect the correct use of the formula since .81 is the predictor's reliability coe�cient.
Answer B: The formula for the relationship between a predictor's reliability and validity requires the square root of the predictor's reliability
coe�cient. An answer of .81 does not re�ect the correct use of the formula since .81 is the predictor's reliability coe�cient.
Answer C: A predictor's validity coe�cient can be no greater than the square root of its reliability coe�cient, so the formula places an upper
limit on the validity coe�cient. The validity coe�cient can be less than the square root of its reliability coe�cient. In this situation, the
predictor's reliability coe�cient is .81, and the square root of .81 is .90. Therefore, the validity coe�cient can be less than .90.

questions.question: In test construction, shrinkage is associated with:
questions.explanation:
In the context of test construction, shrinkage refers to a reduction in the magnitude of a measure's criterion-related validity coe�cient. Cross-
validation refers to validating a predictor with a new sample. The validity coe�cient typically "shrinks" (becomes smaller) on cross-validation
because the chance factors operating in the original sample are not all present in the cross-validation sample.
Answer A: A test has differential validity when it has different validity coe�cients for different groups.
Answer B: Incremental validity refers to the extent to which a predictor increases decision-making accuracy.
Answer D: Process validation describes how a process will continue to meet pre-determined standards.

questions.question: The slope of an item characteristic curve (ICC) indicates which of the following?

options.A: The item's ability to discriminate between high and low achievers
options.C: The susceptibility of the item to social desirability effects
options.D: The probability that the item can be answered correctly by guessing

questions.explanation:
The various item response theory models produce item characteristic curves (ICCs) that provide information on either one, two, or three
parameters—di�culty, discrimination, and probability of guessing correctly. An item's ability to discriminate between high and low achievers is
indicated by the slope of the ICC—the steeper the slope, the greater its discrimination.
Answer B: An item's level of di�culty is indicated by the ability level (charted on the horizontal axis) at which 50% of examinees in the sample
answer the item correctly.
Answer C: The ICC does not measure susceptibility to social desirability.
Answer D: The probability of guessing correctly is indicated by the point at which the ICC intercepts the vertical axis.

questions.question: When assessing the test-retest reliability of your newly developed personality test, you obtain a reliability coe�cient of .80. This means that:

options.A: 80% of variability in test scores is shared variability.
options.B: 64% of variability in test scores is shared variability.
options.C: 80% of variability in test scores is true score variability.
options.D: 64% of variability in test scores is true score variability.

questions.explanation:
Reliability is a measure of the extent to which a test consistently measures the attribute(s) assessed by the test. A reliability coe�cient is
interpreted directly as the proportion of variability in obtained test scores that re�ects true score variability.
Answer A: The reliability coe�cient does not share variability with other measures.
Answer B: The reliability coe�cient is not squared in order to make an interpretation, and the reliability coe�cient does not share variability
with other measures. The value of .64 represents the square of the reliability coe�cient of .80.
Answer D: Although this answer references the reliability coe�cient as a true score of variability, the value of .64 is the square of the reliability
coe�cient of .80. The reliability coe�cient is never squared for interpretation; it is interpreted directly as a measure of true score variability.
